process.title: Name the route, the level and the school
process.description: Analysis and Approaches Higher Level and Applications and Interpretation Standard Level are different courses with different topic lists and different papers. Naming the route, the level and the school tells the tutor which content, which papers and which internal deadlines the plan has to work to.

process.title: Send one marked paper and the exploration status
process.description: A marked mock or past paper classifies the losses, and knowing whether the exploration topic is approved, drafted or not started tells us where the recoverable marks actually are. Those two facts turn a general enquiry into a specific proposal in one message.

process.title: Free trial lesson with a maths specialist
process.description: A trial over live video at no cost, before any payment, with the student doing most of the work. The test afterwards is whether the tutor named something specific about how the marks are being lost. If not, ask for a different tutor at no cost.

process.title: Fix the slot and the block length
process.description: Sessions sit on Gulf Standard Time around the school run from Arabian Ranches or Al Barsha South. The block length follows the calendar: a term-time weekly hour, an exploration push of three or four sessions, or an eight-week paper block before a session.

process.title: Review against the dates, not the feeling
process.description: Every four to six weeks the plan is checked against the exploration deadline, the mock window and the session itself. Session notes record the classified losses and which have closed, so the review is a short factual conversation rather than a general one about effort.

whyPoints.title: The plan has dates on it
whyPoints.description: Route choice, exploration approval, mock window and the session are written down at the start, and the work for each phase differs. A plan without those dates is a standing order, and most families in this belt have paid for one of those before.

whyPoints.title: Paper 1 is drilled without a calculator
whyPoints.description: Non-calculator fluency degrades silently, because school classwork almost always has technology to hand. Short timed non-calculator sets, marked immediately with every error classified as slip or method, is the one drill that reliably moves an Analysis grade.

whyPoints.title: The exploration is treated as the improvable component
whyPoints.description: It carries roughly a fifth of the subject grade and has a deadline a family can still influence, which makes it the highest-return work available in Year 12. Presentation, engagement and reflection are credited separately from the mathematics.

whyPoints.title: Losses are classified before anything is taught
whyPoints.description: Content absence, method loss, timing collapse and misreading feel identical to a student and need different fixes on different timescales. Two timed papers marked by the student produce that classification in a fortnight.

whyPoints.title: Rates on this page are sourced market figures
whyPoints.description: Every AED band is attributed to the provider or cost table that published it. None of them is an IB Gram price list, and no statistic about our own students appears anywhere, because a reader could not verify one.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits are stated, not discovered
whyPoints.description: Analysis and Applications at Standard Level are well covered. Higher Level Analysis is covered. Further Mathematics and some option combinations are thin everywhere, and where that applies you are told with a timescale rather than matched to a generalist.

faqs.question: When in the Diploma should a Mudon family start maths tutoring?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most do. The highest-return window is the first term of Year 12, when the exploration topic is being chosen and non-calculator fluency can still be rebuilt without pressure. The second-best is the summer between Year 11 and Year 12, which is the cheapest useful block in the whole course and almost nobody uses it. Starting in the spring of Year 13 still helps, but by then the work is limited to technique, pacing and marked-script repair, because the exploration is submitted and content gaps cannot be closed securely.

faqs.question: How much of the maths grade does the exploration actually carry?
faqs.answer: Roughly a fifth of the subject grade, with the exact figure set by the current subject guide, which your school's maths department can confirm. What makes it important is not only the share but the fact that its deadline is months away and therefore still influenceable, unlike the papers. It is marked against criteria covering presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics, and students routinely lose marks on the three criteria that are not the mathematics itself.

faqs.question: My son uses a calculator for everything. Is that a problem for Paper 1?
faqs.answer: In Analysis and Approaches, yes, and it is a problem that hides until a mock. Paper 1 is taken without a calculator, so exact-value work, surds, logarithms and three-line algebraic manipulations have to be reliable. School classwork and homework are almost always done with technology to hand, so the fluency degrades without anyone noticing. The fix is short timed non-calculator sets, marked immediately, with every error classified as either a slip or a method problem, because those two need completely different responses.

faqs.question: What makes a good exploration topic rather than an interesting one?
faqs.answer: Accessible mathematics at the student's own level, a question narrow enough that the work fits the expected length, and a genuine reason this student chose it. The test is whether they can say in one sentence what mathematics they will do and why it is theirs. Topics that sound impressive but have no mathematics the student can actually handle cannot be rescued by effort, and topics so broad that the mathematics becomes a survey cannot show engagement. One session on topic choice is worth several on polishing.

faqs.question: Is Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level easier than Analysis?
faqs.answer: Not easier, different. Applications at Higher Level carries substantial statistical content plus matrices, graph theory and complex numbers, and its Paper 3 modelling investigation defeats students who chose the route to avoid calculus. Analysis is harder on manipulation and proof. The right question is fit rather than difficulty: a student who enjoys proof and algebra does better in Analysis, one who prefers interpreting real data does better in Applications. University entry profiles then constrain the choice, and those should be read from the institution's own published requirements.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover maths and physics for a Year 13 in Mudon?
faqs.answer: Often, and the overlap is real: mechanics, fields and induction reuse the same calculus and vector work as Analysis and Approaches, so one subject can reinforce the other instead of competing with it. At Higher Level in both simultaneously the combination is less common, and the honest answer is sometimes two tutors. Either way the scheduling is identical, because no travel has to be arranged between the slots. Ask which papers the tutor has marked in each subject rather than whether they can teach both.

faqs.question: How many maths sessions a week are sensible during term?
faqs.answer: One, in most cases, rising to two in the eight to twelve weeks before a session if the marked scripts justify it. The limiting factor during term is not input but the student's own practice time between sessions, and a second hour that leaves no time to work on the first is wasted money. The exception is a holiday block, where three or four sessions in a week can close a content gap that term time cannot absorb. The marked work decides this, which is why we ask for a script first.

faqs.question: What should we do with the marked mock paper the school sent home?
faqs.answer: Bring it to the first session rather than filing it. A maths mock script separates four failures that feel the same to a student: questions never attempted, method that was right but presented in a way that lost marks, timing collapse visible as an abandoned final page, and a correct method answering the wrong question. Each needs a different fix on a different timescale. The grade tells you the size of the problem; only the annotations tell you its shape, and the shape is what a plan is built on.

faqs.question: How do we practise Paper 3 at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: By rehearsing it whole, two or three times, under full time. Paper 3 is an extended investigation in Analysis and a modelling investigation in Applications, and it rewards structure rather than extra content: reading the entire question before starting, establishing notation, generalising carefully and justifying each step. Students who have never sat one lose marks to a slow unstructured opening and then run out of time. Almost nobody rehearses it, which makes it one of the few places where a small amount of preparation produces a visible change.

faqs.question: Will sessions continue through Ramadan for students in Dubailand?
faqs.answer: Yes, usually moved rather than paused. School days shorten and energy patterns change, and many families in this belt prefer slots after Iftar. Because the lesson arrives over live video with nobody travelling, a time change costs nothing and can be arranged week by week. Fixing those slots early in the month is easier than competing for them later. Where a family would rather pause entirely, the slot can be held and resumed, and the plan is reviewed against the exploration deadline and the session either way.

faqs.question: Does a maths tutor need a licence to teach privately in Dubai?
faqs.answer: The individual does. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own listing shows no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, although no fine schedule is published. A centre with premises needs a separate KHDA permit, which IB Gram does not hold.

faqs.question: What does an eight-week maths block cost at market rates?
faqs.answer: Price it as sixteen sessions rather than as an hourly figure. A qualified subject tutor working online sits at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour in this market, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, and subject specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above with TutorChase publishing AED 270. Multiply the band by sixteen for a planning number. Bestimate's monthly estimates for specialist exam-year support run AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more. These are published market figures with their sources named rather than IB Gram prices.

faqs.question: My daughter is strong in class but underperforms in timed papers. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always execution rather than knowledge. Classwork is untimed, often collaborative and nearly always calculator-assisted, so none of the three things a paper tests are being practised. The specific failures are predictable: no question-order strategy, so the last page is abandoned; no plan line before calculator use, so time is spent searching; and no habit of checking a rearrangement, so one slip ends a question. All three respond to full papers under conditions within a few weeks, which is faster than any content intervention.

faqs.question: Can a tutor check the mathematics in an exploration draft?
faqs.answer: Yes, as feedback on her own work. A tutor can say that a step does not follow, that notation is inconsistent, that a model's assumption has not been stated, that the reflection identifies no limitation, and that a criterion is not being addressed at all. What a tutor must not do is rewrite a section, draft the reflection, edit the document to completion or supply a worked exploration to adapt. The exploration is authenticated by her teacher, and a malpractice finding can cost the Diploma rather than just the marks.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-mudon.closingBody: Before choosing a tutor, write down four dates: the exploration deadline, the mock window, the session, and any family travel in between. Then send the route, the level, the school and one marked paper, and a free trial lesson over live video is arranged before any payment is taken. The plan that comes back will say what the next eight weeks should achieve rather than offering an indefinite weekly hour. Lessons are delivered online on Gulf Standard Time; home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only.

intro.heading: Two things to get right before the first lesson
paragraphs: The first is the course. IB mathematics is two separate subjects, each at two levels, and the four combinations are not interchangeable. Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches is the algebra, functions and calculus route, with a non-calculator paper. Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation is the modelling and statistics route, calculator-permitted throughout. A tutor who teaches one well may be mediocre at the other, and the commonest wasted month in this catchment is a student getting excellent tuition in the wrong route.

Ask the school for the course title as written on the student's record, not the shorthand. "Maths HL" is not an answer. "Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation HL" is. If the student is in the first year and the school has not finalised the route, that conversation is more urgent than tutoring, because engineering and most science degrees expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, while business, social science and several economics routes accept Applications and Interpretation.

The second thing to get right is the hour, and in Muhaisnah that is a logistics problem rather than a preference. Almost no student living here attends school here. The British and IB provision sits in Al Qusais, Mirdif, Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City, which means a journey at both ends of the day. A school finishing at a quarter to three routinely puts a student through a Muhaisnah front door at a quarter past four, and the Al Nahda and Al Ittihad Road peak is what makes the difference.

Mathematics is the subject least tolerant of a badly chosen hour. A student can read a History source at nine in the evening and get something from it. A student attempting integration by substitution at nine in the evening after a long bus journey is generating errors to be unpicked next week. So the slot decision comes first: in this catchment that means six o'clock for most Year 11 and first-year Diploma students, half past seven for second-year students from January once school revision clinics have taken the earlier hours, and Saturday mornings for anyone whose weekdays are genuinely full.

Everything else on this page follows from those two decisions. The route comparison with university expectations attached. The paper structure and weightings at both levels of both routes, so you know what your child is actually sitting. The topics where marks go missing and why. The exploration, criterion by criterion, with its 20 marks and the firm boundary on what a tutor may do with it. The transition from a Middle Years Programme or IGCSE maths background into the Diploma, which is where most of this catchment's difficulty originates. And what the Dubai market charges, attributed to the providers who published the figures.

A note on what this page does not do. It does not promise a grade, and no tutor honestly can: the exploration is marked by the school and moderated, the papers are marked externally, and a student's performance on the day is theirs. What a specialist can change is the number of marks lost for reasons that have nothing to do with mathematical understanding, and in this subject that number is usually large enough to move a grade on its own.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-muhaisnah.programmesIntro: Mathematics support in this catchment is requested at three points in the continuum, and the job is different at each because the assessment model changes completely.

programmes.name: Diploma mathematics
programmes.description: Either Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, at Standard or Higher Level, examined at the end of two years across two or three written papers, plus the exploration at 20%. Standard Level sits two papers of an hour and a half; Higher Level sits two longer papers plus a third worth 20% of the grade.
programmes.countryNote: Almost every Muhaisnah Diploma maths enquiry names a specific breaking point rather than a general difficulty: calculus in the first year, or Paper 3 in the second. That specificity is useful, because it means a short targeted block often does more than a year-long slot.

programmes.name: Middle Years mathematics
programmes.description: Standard or extended mathematics assessed against four criteria, each marked out of 8 and converted to a 1-7 grade. Criterion C asks students to communicate mathematically and criterion D to apply mathematics in real-life contexts, which is why a student with fluent arithmetic can still sit mid-band.
programmes.countryNote: Families arriving in Mirdif or Festival City schools from a CBSE or British background read a 5 out of 8 as a near-fail and panic. The fixable issue is almost always presentation and process description rather than mathematics, and it responds quickly to being taught deliberately.

programmes.name: IGCSE mathematics, as the route into the Diploma
programmes.description: Cambridge 0580 or Pearson 4MA1, tiered, examined externally. The content overlaps substantially with the opening units of Diploma mathematics, and a student entering the Diploma from a Core or Foundation tier faces a genuinely steep first term, particularly in Analysis and Approaches.
programmes.countryNote: This is the most common origin of Diploma maths difficulty in eastern Dubai. A student who was comfortable on the Extended tier adapts; a student who scraped through on Core and was placed in Analysis and Approaches is carrying an algebra gap into a calculus course, and the honest fix is foundational work before the term starts.

programmes.name: The route decision itself
programmes.ageRange: Taken in Year 11 or early DP1
programmes.description: Not a programme but the decision that governs everything else. It is usually made by the school in consultation with the family, on the basis of prior attainment and intended destination, and it is extremely difficult to reverse once the second year begins because the content diverges rather than overlapping.
programmes.countryNote: When a Muhaisnah family contacts us during the route decision rather than after it, the most valuable hour is spent on the university requirement for the intended destination rather than on mathematics. That conversation is free at the consultation and it has saved several families a wasted year.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-muhaisnah.subjectsIntro: Diploma mathematics breaks into identifiable topic areas, and difficulty concentrates in a few of them. These are the ones Muhaisnah enquiries name.

subjects.name: Number and algebra
subjects.description: Sequences, series, exponentials and logarithms, with binomial expansion and at Higher Level proof and complex numbers. Weak index and surd manipulation here propagates into every later topic, which is why a diagnostic always starts in this area.

subjects.name: Functions
subjects.description: Domain and range, transformations, composite and inverse functions. The commonest loss is sketching without intercepts, asymptotes or turning points labelled, which costs method marks even when the shape is right.

subjects.name: Geometry and trigonometry
subjects.description: Trigonometric identities and equations in Analysis and Approaches; three-dimensional geometry and vectors at Higher Level. Students lose marks giving a single solution where the interval demands several.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: Distributions, correlation and regression, hypothesis testing in Applications and Interpretation. The recurring failure is a correct calculator output with no interpretation sentence attached, which is precisely what the mark scheme asks for.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.description: Differentiation and integration techniques, kinematics, and at Analysis and Approaches Higher Level substitution, parts and differential equations. This is where most first-year Diploma grades in this catchment fall, and where recovery takes longest.

subjects.name: Paper 3 problem solving
subjects.description: Two extended investigative questions worth 20% of the grade, requiring sustained reasoning across a single scenario. Students meet nothing like it at IGCSE or in the Middle Years Programme, and it is almost entirely a technique to be practised rather than content to be learned.

subjects.name: The mathematical exploration
subjects.description: A piece of personal mathematics marked out of 20 across five criteria and worth 20% of the grade. More marks are lost here to a poorly chosen topic than to mathematical error, and the choice is made months before the writing.

subjects.name: Graphic display calculator technique
subjects.levels: Essential in AI, significant in AA
subjects.description: Fluency with the permitted calculator is examinable in effect: students lose time and accuracy on tasks the device does instantly. Applications and Interpretation permits it on every paper, Analysis and Approaches does not on Paper 1.

subjects.name: Mathematical communication
subjects.description: Notation, defined variables, stated methods and units. A correct answer with unstated working loses method marks in every paper, and this is the single most teachable gain available to a student in the first weeks of tutoring.

subjects.name: Modelling in context
subjects.description: Choosing and justifying a model, fitting it, then criticising it. Applications and Interpretation students frequently fit without justifying and conclude without criticising, which removes the marks the question was designed around.

subjects.name: Proof
subjects.description: Direct proof, contradiction, and proof by induction. Students who can follow a proof often cannot construct one, and the gap is structural rather than mathematical: knowing what a proof must establish and in what order.

subjects.name: Sequences for financial applications
subjects.description: Compound interest, annuities, amortisation and depreciation. Straightforward content that is frequently under-practised because it appears easy, and then costs marks on precision of rounding and on reading the period correctly.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-muhaisnah.regionsTitle: School end times and the maths slot, community by community
dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-muhaisnah.regionsIntro: Where the student goes to school decides when mathematics can usefully be taught. These are the communities involved and what each does to the clock.

regions.name: Muhaisnah
regions.note: Four sub-communities on Al Awir Road with no local IB or British secondary provision, so the maths slot is always set by a journey rather than by a walk home.

regions.name: Al Qusais
regions.note: The commonest school destination from Muhaisnah and the one most affected by the Al Nahda bottleneck. Students from here are usually home between four and half past, so six o'clock is the realistic earliest maths slot.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: Short drive, slow gates. Pick-up queues around the retail centre run until about four, which pushes the first workable session to half past six for most families.

regions.name: Al Garhoud
regions.note: The shortest run in this cluster, west along Al Rebat Street. Students schooling here get home early enough that half past five genuinely works, which matters for calculus.

regions.name: Dubai Festival City
regions.note: Staggered pick-ups by year group mean an older sibling can arrive an hour after a younger one. Plan the maths slot around the later arrival, not the earlier.

regions.name: Al Warqa
regions.note: Long multi-community bus loops serve the schools here, so the last student dropped can be forty minutes behind the first. Ask the school which end of the route your child sits on.

regions.name: Al Nahda
regions.note: The single biggest variable in this catchment's afternoon. Families living on this boundary should plan half past seven rather than anything earlier, and should not expect a six o'clock session to survive the term.

regions.name: Al Mizhar
regions.note: Beyond Mirdif with long bus routes. Distance is modest but the timetable, not the map, decides the slot, and the bus timetable is obtainable from the school.

regions.name: Nad Al Hamar
regions.note: Quick access to Festival City and Rashidiya schools. One of the few parts of this cluster where a half past five mathematics session reliably holds.

regions.name: International City
regions.note: Long journeys in both directions. Saturday morning maths sessions outperform weekday ones here by a wide margin, and families who accept that early keep continuity.

schoolClusters.city: Festival City, Garhoud and Mirdif
schoolClusters.note: Where the IB mathematics taught to Muhaisnah students actually happens, including one full continuum school. End times from this group are earlier than from Al Qusais, which widens the choice of maths slot.

schoolClusters.city: Al Qusais and Al Warqa
schoolClusters.note: The nearer school ring, heavier on British and Indian curricula, feeding IGCSE mathematics that becomes Diploma mathematics two years later. Students we support from this catchment attend schools across both clusters.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation: the decision that outlasts school
paragraphs: This is the most consequential choice in IB mathematics and it is frequently made on the wrong information. The two courses share a few topic headings and diverge sharply in emphasis. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and analytical, builds towards calculus, and includes a paper sat without a calculator. Applications and Interpretation is statistical and modelling-led, permits a calculator throughout, and asks students to justify and criticise models rather than to prove results.

Neither is easier. They are differently hard, and the student who thrives in one may genuinely struggle in the other. What is not symmetrical is the university consequence. Engineering, physics, mathematics and many pure science programmes expect Analysis and Approaches, commonly at Higher Level. Business, management, social sciences, psychology and a number of economics programmes accept Applications and Interpretation. Medicine varies by country and institution and must be checked individually rather than assumed.

The practical instruction for a Muhaisnah family is to check the actual entry requirement of the actual destination before the route is locked, and to check it on the university's own admissions page rather than on a forum. Requirements are stated by subject and level, and a page that says "IB mathematics" without specifying is not the page to rely on. If the intended destination is unclear, the lower-risk choice is usually the one that keeps more doors open, which for science-leaning students means Analysis and Approaches.

If the route is already wrong for the target, the conversation is about alternative entry paths, foundation years or a different destination, not about tutoring harder. We would say that at the consultation. The table sets out the comparison across the dimensions that matter, and the last column is the one to read if your child is currently in the first year and the decision is still live.

sections.heading: What your child is actually sitting: papers, durations and weightings
paragraphs: Ask a tutor to recite this from memory before you book them. A specialist will. The structure is consistent in shape across both routes and differs by level: Standard Level sits two written papers plus the exploration, Higher Level sits three written papers plus the exploration. The exploration is 20% of the grade in all four combinations, which surprises families who have treated it as a side project.

At Standard Level the two papers each carry 40% and run an hour and a half. The difference between the routes is the calculator: Analysis and Approaches Paper 1 is sat without one, while Applications and Interpretation permits one on both. At Higher Level the two main papers each carry 30% and run two hours, and the third paper carries 20% in an hour, consisting of two extended problem-solving questions.

That third paper deserves separate planning, because nothing in a student's prior experience resembles it. Two long investigative questions on a single scenario, requiring sustained reasoning and the confidence to continue when an early part has gone wrong. Students who have prepared only by topic revision meet it cold and lose a fifth of the grade in an hour. A bounded block of timed practice is the standard remedy and it works.

Weightings and durations are revised when a subject guide is reissued, so confirm the detail against the current guide for your child's cohort, which the school's IB coordinator can provide. What will not change is the planning implication: the exploration is a fifth of the grade and is entirely within the student's control months before any exam, which makes it the most reliably recoverable component on the whole course.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go missing
paragraphs: Most students losing marks in IB mathematics are not failing to understand the mathematics. They are losing method marks to presentation, losing accuracy marks to rounding, and losing interpretation marks by stopping at a number. All three are teachable in weeks rather than terms, which is why a diagnostic session on marked scripts is worth more than a month of topic coverage.

The presentation losses are the easiest to fix and the most consistently ignored. An unstated method, a derivative taken without naming the rule, a variable used but never defined, a sketch without intercepts or asymptotes labelled, a final answer given without units. Each costs one or two marks and they accumulate into a grade. A student who writes as though a marker needs convincing rather than as though the answer is obvious gains most of this back inside a term.

The accuracy losses cluster around rounding and premature approximation. Rounding an intermediate value and carrying it forward converts a correct method into a wrong answer, and a final answer given to the wrong degree of accuracy loses a mark that the mathematics had already earned. Applications and Interpretation students compound this with calculator-display habits, reading off more or fewer figures than the question requires.

The interpretation losses are the largest and the most route-specific. A regression line calculated and left unexplained, a correlation coefficient stated without comment on strength or validity, a model fitted without justification and concluded without criticism. These are the marks Applications and Interpretation is designed around, and a student who has learned the mechanics without the commentary is capped well below where their mathematics would place them. In Analysis and Approaches the analogous loss is in proof: following an argument is not constructing one, and the structural habits of a proof have to be taught explicitly.
bullets: Method marks: state the rule, define the variable, show the step
Sketches: intercepts, asymptotes and turning points labelled every time
Rounding: never carry an approximated intermediate value forward
Trigonometric equations: give every solution in the stated interval
Statistics: a number is not an answer until it has a sentence attached
Proof: know what must be established and in what order before starting

sections.heading: Choosing the maths hour: what works from this catchment and what does not
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject where the wrong hour does the most damage, because errors made while tired have to be unpicked rather than simply repeated. So the slot is not a scheduling detail, it is part of the teaching plan. The table below sets out the hours available to a Muhaisnah family, what each is realistically good for in mathematics specifically, and how often it survives a full term.

The headline is that six o'clock and half past seven carry nearly all our mathematics bookings from this catchment, and the half past four slot families instinctively request is the one most often abandoned by week five. A student arriving at a quarter past four from Al Qusais cannot be learning integration at half past, and the session becomes a conversation about homework instead, which is a different and much cheaper product.

Two local variables belong in the decision. Maghrib prayer timing moves through the year and sits awkwardly against a six o'clock slot in winter months. During Ramadan, school days shorten and Iftar reorganises the evening entirely; families who agree the Ramadan arrangement in advance keep continuity through the month, and those who do not generally lose it and restart in a worse position. Post-Iftar mathematics works well for some households and not at all for others, and it is worth asking the student rather than assuming.

The last column is the one to act on. A slot that holds for twenty-eight weeks beats a theoretically better slot that collapses nine times, because continuity is most of what weekly mathematics support delivers. If no weekday hour genuinely survives, take Saturday morning and stop fighting the timetable: a nine-thirty start on a Saturday is the most reliable mathematics hour available in this part of Dubai.

sections.heading: The exploration: 20 marks, five criteria, and a firm boundary
paragraphs: The mathematical exploration is worth 20% of the final grade, is marked out of 20 across five criteria, and is almost entirely within the student's control. It is therefore the single most reliably recoverable component on the course, and the one most often treated as an administrative task to be completed at the last possible moment. Families who understand the mark allocation early get the benefit; families who discover it in the final weeks do not.

More marks are lost to topic choice than to mathematical error. A topic that is too large cannot be explored properly in the space available; a topic that is too small leaves nothing to say; a topic the student has no genuine connection to makes the personal engagement criterion unreachable. Testing topic viability is the first job, it takes one session, and it is the highest-return hour available in the entire course.

The boundary on help is firm and we state it plainly. A tutor may explain what each criterion asks for, interrogate the topic and the mathematics, point out that a section does not yet meet a descriptor, and model the technique on an unrelated example. A tutor may not write, restructure or complete any part of the exploration. After a good session the student holds three specific problems to fix and the document contains no sentence or line of mathematics the tutor supplied.

The table gives the criteria with marks and the loss we see most often against each. Use it as a checklist with your child: pick the criterion with the largest allocation, ask them to show you where their draft serves it, and if they cannot point at it, that is the next session's work. Confirm the exact descriptors against the current subject guide, which the school's IB coordinator can supply.

sections.heading: From MYP or IGCSE into Diploma mathematics: the real gap
paragraphs: Most Diploma mathematics difficulty in this catchment starts before the Diploma. A student arrives from the Middle Years Programme or from IGCSE with a grade that looked acceptable and a set of habits that are not sufficient, and the first-year course does not pause to rebuild them. The gap is specific and it is diagnosable in a single session on marked work.

Coming from IGCSE, the gap is usually algebraic fluency and the expectation of independent practice. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 reward accurate execution of recognisable question types; Diploma papers reward adaptation to an unfamiliar framing. A student entering Analysis and Approaches from the Core or Foundation tier faces the steepest version of this, and the honest fix is foundational algebra before term starts rather than remedial calculus in November.

Coming from the Middle Years Programme, the gap is different. Criterion-marked tasks reward process description and real-world application, and often permit a calculator and multiple attempts. The Diploma asks for speed, by-hand fluency in Analysis and Approaches, and performance under examination conditions. Students who were strong on criteria C and D can be genuinely unprepared for Paper 1 without anybody having noticed.

The practical sequence we recommend for a Muhaisnah family in this position is unglamorous. Get the most recent marked work, spend one session diagnosing which of the three gaps is present, fix the foundational one first even if it feels like going backwards, and only then move to the current unit. Families who insist on starting with the unit the student is failing now generally spend twice as long, because the failure was never about that unit.
bullets: From Core or Foundation tier into Analysis and Approaches: algebra first, always
From Extended or Higher tier: the gap is adaptation, not content
From the Middle Years Programme: by-hand fluency and timed performance
In every case: diagnose from marked work before buying a block of hours
Fix the foundation even when it feels like going backwards

sections.heading: What Diploma mathematics support costs in eastern Dubai
paragraphs: Mathematics is the most tutored subject in this market, which keeps supply reasonable and rates mid-band rather than scarce. Across the published Dubai figures, qualified subject tutors working online sit roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with one agency publishing IB from AED 200. IB and A Level specialists run roughly AED 200 to 450 and above, with one UK agency publishing AED 270 and a premium examiner-branded provider publishing AED 650. In-home visits are quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 with travel included.

Per grade moved, mathematics is often the better value in a Diploma student's basket, because the losses are specific. A student dropping method marks and rounding accuracy can be visibly better in six weeks, which is not true of a student who needs to rebuild two years of reading in a literature subject. That makes a bounded block a sensible purchase here, and it is how we would advise most families in this catchment to start.

The expensive pattern is the opposite: an open-ended weekly slot bought in panic in the second year, with no stated target, renewed monthly out of uncertainty. Published monthly estimates for specialist exam-year support run roughly AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for a weekly hour, so an unevaluated engagement across a year is a substantial sum for something nobody is measuring.

On our own figure: it is agreed at the consultation once the route, level and cadence are known, because a weekly Standard Level slot and a Paper 3 intensive are not the same product. We sit in the qualified-specialist part of the bands above, not the budget part. The trial lesson is free, nothing is charged before it, and if the marked work suggests a short block rather than a year-long slot we will say so even though it is the smaller sale.

sections.heading: Starting mathematics support from Muhaisnah
paragraphs: Send three things. The full course title and level as the school writes it, so we match the route correctly. The most recent marked paper, which tells a mathematics specialist in two minutes whether the problem is method marks, accuracy, interpretation or genuine content gaps. And the school's weekly timetable, including the late afternoons, so the slot is chosen rather than guessed.

We then propose a specialist in that route at that level and a free trial lesson in a slot the school run can survive. Ask the tutor to recite the papers, durations and weightings for your child's exact combination. A specialist does it from memory in under a minute. Ask also what they will refuse to do with the exploration, and expect a firm answer without prompting.

After the trial we agree one capability to be true by session six, expressed in a way you can check from a marked script. For mathematics that is usually mechanical: stating methods without being reminded, labelling sketches completely, carrying unrounded intermediate values, or attaching an interpretation sentence to every statistical result. At session six you look at the work, not at a conversation.

One last suggestion specific to this catchment. If your child is in the first year of the Diploma, spend the first block on the exploration topic and on method-mark discipline rather than on the current unit. Both are cheap, both are entirely within the student's control, and both pay back across the whole two years. Almost every family who starts the other way round asks us in the second year why nobody mentioned the exploration earlier.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child is on Maths AA or AI?
faqs.answer: Ask the school for the full course title as it appears on the student's record, and ask the mathematics teacher rather than the student. "Maths HL" is not an answer; "Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation HL" is. It matters because the two courses differ in emphasis, in calculator rules and in what universities accept. Analysis and Approaches sits Paper 1 without a calculator and builds towards calculus and proof; Applications and Interpretation permits a calculator throughout and is statistical and modelling-led. A tutor who is strong in one is not automatically useful in the other.

faqs.question: Which IB maths course do UAE and overseas universities want?
faqs.answer: It depends on the programme, which is why it has to be checked on the university's own admissions page rather than assumed. Engineering, physics, mathematics and many pure science degrees commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level. Business, management, social sciences and several economics programmes accept Applications and Interpretation. Medicine varies by country and institution. If the destination is still open, the route that keeps more doors available is usually Analysis and Approaches for science-leaning students. Changing route after the first year is generally not possible, so the check belongs before the decision.

faqs.question: What are the papers and weightings for IB maths at each level?
faqs.answer: Standard Level sits two papers, each an hour and a half and each worth 40%, plus the exploration at 20%. Higher Level sits three: two papers of two hours at 30% each, a third paper of an hour at 20% consisting of two extended problem-solving questions, plus the same exploration at 20%. Analysis and Approaches Paper 1 is sat without a calculator; Applications and Interpretation permits one throughout. Confirm the current detail against your child's subject guide, which the school's IB coordinator can supply, because structures are revised when a guide is reissued.

faqs.question: What exactly is Paper 3 and why does everyone worry about it?
faqs.answer: Paper 3 is sat only at Higher Level, runs an hour, carries 20% of the grade, and consists of two extended investigative questions built on a single scenario each. Nothing a student has met at IGCSE or in the Middle Years Programme resembles it: it rewards sustained reasoning and the nerve to keep going after an early part has gone wrong, rather than recognition of a familiar question type. Students who prepare only by revising topics meet it cold and lose a fifth of the grade in sixty minutes. Timed practice against the published scheme is the standard remedy.

faqs.question: My child understands the maths but keeps losing marks. What is happening?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly method, accuracy and interpretation losses rather than content. Method marks go missing when a rule is used without being named, a variable is used without being defined, or a sketch lacks intercepts and asymptotes. Accuracy marks go when an intermediate value is rounded and carried forward. Interpretation marks go when a calculated figure is left without a sentence explaining it, which is specifically what Applications and Interpretation questions are designed around. All three are visible in a marked script and all three are fixable within a term.

faqs.question: When should the exploration be started?
faqs.answer: Earlier than almost anyone does. It carries 20% of the subject grade and is marked out of 20 across five criteria, and more marks are lost to a poorly chosen topic than to any mathematical error in the writing. One session spent testing whether a topic is viable, genuinely connected to the student, and of appropriate mathematical level is the highest-return hour on the whole course. Families who reach it in the second year find most of the available marks already out of reach, because personal engagement and reflection cannot be retro-fitted to a topic chosen for convenience.

faqs.question: Can a tutor check the exploration before submission?
faqs.answer: A tutor can read the student's own draft against the five criteria and say precisely which descriptor is not yet met, question whether the mathematics is at the level of the course, and test the reflection for genuine critical discussion rather than a closing paragraph. A tutor cannot write, restructure or complete any part of it. After a session the student should hold three specific problems and the document should contain nothing the tutor supplied. Providers who will write an exploration exist; using one puts the student in front of an IB malpractice panel.

faqs.question: What time should a maths session start if my child schools in Mirdif?
faqs.answer: Half past six is the realistic earliest. School gates around Mirdif stay congested until roughly four, and a student arriving in Muhaisnah at a quarter past four needs to eat and change before learning anything. For new content, six o'clock or half past six works; for timed practice, half past seven is better because it mimics nothing about exam conditions but leaves the student alert. Mathematics is the subject least tolerant of a tired student, because errors made while exhausted have to be unpicked rather than simply repeated next week.

faqs.question: Is online maths tutoring workable without a shared whiteboard?
faqs.answer: It needs a way for the tutor to see the student's written work as it is produced, which is not negotiable for mathematics. A tablet with a stylus is ideal. A phone propped so the page is visible works. A shared document is fine for statistics and modelling but poor for by-hand algebra. What does not work is a student describing their working aloud while the tutor guesses, and families who solve this in the first week get noticeably more from every subsequent session.

faqs.question: My child came into the Diploma from IGCSE Core and is struggling. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: With algebra, even though it feels like going backwards. A student who was comfortable on the Extended or Higher tier adapts to Diploma mathematics within a term; a student who passed on Core or Foundation and was placed in Analysis and Approaches is carrying an index, surd and manipulation gap into a calculus course that will not pause. Diagnosing that from marked work takes one session. Fixing the foundation first is faster overall than attacking the unit they are currently failing, because the failure was never really about that unit.

faqs.question: How much does an IB maths tutor cost in this part of Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai figures put qualified subject tutors working online at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with one agency publishing IB from AED 200. IB and A Level specialists run roughly AED 200 to 450 and above, with one UK agency publishing AED 270 and a premium examiner-branded provider publishing AED 650. In-home visits are quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 with travel included. Those belong to the providers named, collected in October 2026. Mathematics is well supplied in this market, which keeps rates mid-band rather than scarce.

faqs.question: Does my child need a tutor for both years of the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and buying two years of weekly support without evaluation is the expensive pattern in this market. A better shape is a bounded first-year block on method-mark discipline and the exploration topic, then nothing, then a second-year block on timed technique and Paper 3 if the marked work says it is needed. Published monthly estimates for specialist exam-year support run roughly AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for a weekly hour, so an unevaluated two-year engagement is a large sum nobody is measuring.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover maths and physics for a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: This is the one pairing where a single specialist genuinely works, because the technique overlap is real: both reward stated method, careful algebra and interpretation of graphs. It still requires a tutor who teaches both courses habitually rather than one who is willing to attempt the second. Ask them to recite the assessment structure for each, separately. If the answer is confident for mathematics and vague for physics, book the mathematics and find a physics specialist, because the vagueness will show up in the second year.

faqs.question: Will sessions still run during Ramadan and school holidays?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing agreed in advance rather than improvised. School days shorten in Ramadan and Iftar reorganises the evening, so a six o'clock mathematics slot that worked in November sits awkwardly. Post-Iftar sessions suit some households and late-morning sessions on non-school days suit others, and it is worth asking the student which they would actually attend. Holidays are often the best time for foundational work, because there is no competing homework and a student can rebuild algebra without also keeping up with the current unit.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-nad-al-hamar.tutorsIntro: Each tutor here teaches one of the two IB Mathematics courses at a stated level. Ask which topic area they are strongest in and which they would not claim; a specialist answers that immediately, and a generalist changes the subject.

intro.heading: Teach the syllabus, not the subject
paragraphs: IB Mathematics is organised into five numbered topic areas, and both courses share the numbering while differing substantially in content inside it. Topic one is number and algebra. Topic two is functions. Topic three is geometry and trigonometry. Topic four is statistics and probability. Topic five is calculus. Analysis and Approaches weights topics one, two, three and five heavily and treats topic four more lightly. Applications and Interpretation does close to the reverse, with topic four carrying a large share and calculus trimmed to what a modelling course needs.

That structure matters because it is how a tutor should diagnose. A student described as bad at maths is almost never bad at all five. More commonly they are fluent in topic one, shaky in topic two where composite and inverse functions live, confident in topic three until the triangle stops being right-angled, and lost in topic five the moment the chain rule has to be recognised rather than applied to a labelled example. Naming the topic area turns a vague complaint into a plan.

The second thing a maths page should cover and almost none do is command terms. The syllabus uses a defined set of instructions, and they are not interchangeable. Show that means produce a complete argument to a stated conclusion. Hence means use the previous part. Deduce means derive from something already established. Verify means substitute and check. Students who treat all of these as solve lose the final mark on question after question while believing their answers were right, which is the most frustrating form of mark loss there is.

Third is Paper 3, which exists only at Higher Level, carries twenty per cent of the grade, and is a different kind of assessment from the other two papers. It is a sustained investigation in an unfamiliar context, where later parts depend on earlier ones and the reward is for reasoning rather than recall. Most schools reach it late in DP2 because the syllabus has to be covered first, which means most students meet it with a term to go. Starting it earlier is the single most useful scheduling decision available to a Higher Level student.

Nad Al Hamar is a residential district on the eastern side of Dubai, between the Ras Al Khor sanctuary and the Dubai-Al Ain Road, and its children travel out to schools in Festival City, Mirdif, Al Warqa, Al Qusais and Academic City. There is no Diploma school inside the district and very few resident maths specialists, so a search by proximity returns the wrong sort of list. Teaching here is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE, because home tutoring is a service we run in India only.

subjects.name: Topic 1: Number and algebra
subjects.levels: AA and AI, SL and HL
subjects.description: Sequences and series, exponents and logarithms, the binomial theorem, and at Higher Level proof, complex numbers and systems of equations in AA, matrices and graph theory in AI. The foundation on which topics two and five rest, and where a hidden weakness does the most downstream damage.

subjects.name: Topic 2: Functions
subjects.levels: AA and AI, SL and HL
subjects.description: Function notation, domain and range, composite and inverse functions, transformations of graphs, and at Higher Level rational and reciprocal functions. The single most common site of unseen weakness, because students can use functions long before they can reason about them.

subjects.name: Topic 3: Geometry and trigonometry
subjects.levels: AA and AI, SL and HL
subjects.description: Non-right-angled triangles, radian measure, trigonometric identities and equations, and at Higher Level vectors in AA and three-dimensional geometry in AI. The point of failure is almost always the move away from right-angled triangles and SOHCAHTOA.

subjects.name: Topic 4: Statistics and probability
subjects.levels: Light in AA, heavy in AI
subjects.description: Descriptive statistics, probability, the binomial and normal distributions, and in AI at Higher Level hypothesis testing and the chi-squared distribution. The content that catches students who chose Applications and Interpretation expecting a lighter course.

subjects.name: Topic 5: Calculus
subjects.levels: Heavy in AA, trimmed in AI
subjects.description: Differentiation and integration, the chain, product and quotient rules, kinematics, and at Higher Level in AA integration by substitution and parts, differential equations and Maclaurin series. Recognition of which rule applies, rather than execution, is where marks go.

subjects.name: The mathematical exploration
subjects.description: An individual investigation worth twenty per cent of the grade, marked by the school against five criteria and externally moderated. Depth of mathematics relative to the course level carries the most marks, which is why a thin topic cannot be rescued by good presentation.

subjects.name: Paper 3, Higher Level only
subjects.description: One extended investigation in an unfamiliar context, roughly an hour, twenty per cent of the grade. Later parts depend on earlier ones, so an early error propagates. Rewards sustained reasoning and penalises students trained only on short structured questions.

subjects.name: Command terms
subjects.description: A defined vocabulary, not stylistic variation. Show that, hence, deduce, verify, justify, determine and find each require something specific, and a student who reads them all as solve forfeits the final mark on questions they otherwise answered correctly.

subjects.name: The graphic display calculator
subjects.description: A skill assessed in practice if not in name. Solver functions, statistical modes, intersections, numerical integration and matrix operations decide whether a student finishes Paper 2, and menu fluency on the student's own model is worth minutes per paper.

sections.heading: The five topic areas, and what differs between the two courses
paragraphs: Both IB Mathematics courses use the same five numbered topic areas, which is why families assume they are versions of one subject. They are not. The numbering is shared and the content inside each number diverges quickly, particularly at Higher Level, where the Analysis and Approaches extension runs into complex numbers, vectors, integration techniques and series, while the Applications and Interpretation extension runs into matrices, graph theory and inferential statistics.

A tutor who has taught one course and not the other will be competent in the shared material and genuinely out of their depth in the extension. This is not a reflection on them; it is a structural fact about a subject that splits. The practical consequence for a parent is that the first question to ask is which course, and the second is which level, and a tutor who answers both vaguely should be passed over. A Nad Al Hamar family with no local specialist to choose from gains most from this test, because the online pool is large enough for it to be worth applying.

The topic-area frame is also the fastest route to a diagnosis. Instead of asking whether a student is good at maths, ask which of the five they can do under timed conditions. Most students who look uniformly weak are strong in topic one, insecure in topic two, fine in topic three until the triangle changes shape, and unable to recognise which calculus rule applies in topic five. Each of those has a different remedy, and three of them are quick.

The table below sets the two courses side by side across the five areas. It is the single most useful thing a parent can read before an options meeting, because the decision that follows from it, Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, constrains degree choices for the next five years and is usually made in fifteen minutes.

sections.heading: Command terms: the marks a correct answer still loses
paragraphs: The IB uses a defined vocabulary of instructions and expects students to read it precisely. This is the single most recoverable source of lost marks in the whole subject, because the student usually already knows the mathematics. A question that says show that requires a complete argument ending at the stated result, and a student who starts from the result and works backwards has not shown it. A question that says hence requires the previous part to be used, and a student who begins again from first principles throws away the connection being tested.

Deduce requires a conclusion drawn from something already established, which means the preceding work must be referenced rather than repeated. Verify means substitute the given value and demonstrate the equality, which is quicker than solving and is marked differently. Justify requires a reason attached to an answer, and an unjustified correct answer scores the answer mark only. Determine and find are the more open instructions and still require working, because method marks exist independently of the final answer.

The diagnostic for this problem is simple and parents can run it themselves. Look at a marked paper and find the questions where the working is right and the mark is not full. If several of those questions begin with show that, hence or justify, the problem is command terms rather than content, and it can be substantially fixed in three or four sessions by a tutor who makes the student underline the instruction before writing anything.

The reason this matters disproportionately in Dubai is that students arrive in the Diploma from IGCSE and MYP, where the command vocabulary is different and less strictly applied. A student who scored well at sixteen on procedural fluency meets a system that pays for communicated reasoning, and nobody tells them the rules have changed. sections.heading: Paper 3: anatomy of a Higher Level investigation
paragraphs: Paper 3 is sat only at Higher Level, carries twenty per cent of the grade, and runs for about an hour on one or two extended investigations. It is unlike Papers 1 and 2 in structure and in what it rewards. The context is unfamiliar by design, the parts build on each other, and the later parts generalise what the earlier ones established. A student who has practised only short structured questions will recognise none of this and will treat each part as a separate exercise, which is exactly the wrong approach.

The internal logic is worth teaching explicitly. An investigation typically opens with concrete cases, asks the student to notice a pattern, then asks for a conjecture, then asks for a proof or justification, then extends the context and asks whether the result still holds. Each stage has a different mark profile. The concrete cases are cheap marks and should be done quickly and accurately. The conjecture must be stated precisely, because a vaguely worded pattern cannot be proved. The proof or justification carries the heaviest weighting.

The single most useful technique for this paper is recovery. Because parts depend on earlier ones, a student who gets part b wrong is at risk of losing c, d and e as well. The remedy is to carry the result forward anyway, state the assumption, and continue, because follow-through credit exists and a blank page earns nothing. Students have to be taught that explicitly; the instinct is to stop and go back, which consumes the clock and produces an unfinished paper.

The scheduling point is the practical one. Schools reach Paper 3 late because the syllabus must be covered first, which leaves most Higher Level students meeting it in the spring with everything else happening at once. A student who begins fortnightly investigation practice in the first term of DP2 will have sat eight or ten of them before their school sets the first, and the difference in that paper is larger than anything else an hour a fortnight buys.

sections.heading: Calculator skills, paper by paper
paragraphs: The graphic display calculator is assessed in effect even though it is not a topic. At Analysis and Approaches, Paper 1 is sat without it, which means every manipulation has to be done by hand under time pressure. At Applications and Interpretation, technology is permitted throughout, which changes the nature of the preparation entirely: the question is no longer whether the student can do the algebra but whether they can drive the machine efficiently and interpret what it returns.

The specific skills differ by paper and by course, and they are teachable in minutes rather than hours once someone identifies which are missing. Fraction and exact-value entry. Storing an answer and recalling it rather than retyping a rounded version, which is the commonest source of accumulated rounding error. Finding intersections rather than solving algebraically when the question permits. Statistical modes for one and two-variable data. Numerical integration. Matrix entry at Applications and Interpretation Higher Level. Degree and radian mode, which silently ruins trigonometric answers.

Teaching this over video is better than teaching it beside someone, which is counterintuitive until you have seen it. The tutor shares an emulator or the matching software on screen, so the menu path appears at a readable size and can be repeated while the student follows on their own handheld model, which is the one they will take into the examination hall. Sitting side by side, the student watches a small screen at an angle.

The rule we apply is that ten minutes of every session goes on calculator work until it stops being a limiting factor, and then it stops. A competent student who navigates slowly will not finish Paper 2, and an unfinished paper costs more marks than any single topic gap. For Analysis and Approaches students the mirror-image rule applies: for Paper 1 preparation the calculator is put away entirely, because the paper will not have it.

sections.heading: Proof, and why it unsettles students who were strong at sixteen
paragraphs: Proof is where Analysis and Approaches stops resembling anything a student met at IGCSE or in MYP. At Standard Level the demands are modest. At Higher Level, proof by induction, proof by contradiction and disproof by counterexample are examinable, and all three ask for a style of writing rather than a calculation. A student who has spent five years producing answers is being asked to produce an argument, and the transition is genuinely difficult for able students who have never needed to justify anything.

Induction has a fixed shape and can be taught as a template without that being a dishonest shortcut: establish the base case, assume the statement for an arbitrary case, prove it for the next, then conclude. The marks sit in the inductive step and in the explicit statement of the assumption, and the commonest loss is a student who performs the algebra of the step without stating what was assumed, which makes the argument incomplete even though every line is correct.

Contradiction is harder because the student must choose what to negate, and counterexample is easy once a student accepts that a single case is sufficient, which many resist because it feels like insufficient work. These three take perhaps four sessions to put in place and they recur, so the return is high. They also feed directly into Paper 3, where the justification stage is frequently a proof in all but name.

There is a wider point here about what a maths tutor is for. A student who is fluent and scoring poorly needs technique and command terms. A student who is accurate and slow needs calculator work and pacing. A student who cannot write an argument needs proof teaching, and that is a different activity from going through more questions. Diagnosing which of the three is in front of you takes one session, and skipping that step is how families spend a term on the wrong thing.

sections.heading: Past papers, used so that they count
paragraphs: Most students use past papers badly, which is a shame because it is the highest-value revision activity available. Doing a paper without timing it produces a false sense of security. Doing one and only checking the final answers skips the method marks, which is where most of the loss sits. Doing one and not recording what went wrong means the same error recurs in the next paper and the one after, and the student concludes they are not good at maths rather than that they have one unaddressed habit.

The method that works is unglamorous. Sit the paper under real conditions, timed, with the correct calculator position for the paper in question. Mark it against the mark scheme without charity, and for each lost mark record a category: method not known, method known but misapplied, arithmetic or accuracy, command term, or ran out of time. Count the categories. The largest category is what the next three sessions are about, and it is usually not the one the student expected.

A note on access. We do not host or supply past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents or grade-boundary tables. They belong to the IB, and your child's school has legitimate access to the assessment material through its own channels. A tutor works from that material inside a session, which is normal practice, and we cite the official sources rather than reproducing them. Any site offering a download library of boards' material is distributing someone else's property, and for unreleased material it is a malpractice exposure.

The other note is about frequency. One paper a fortnight, fully marked and categorised, beats three papers a week that are half-marked and never reviewed. The marking and the review are where the learning is; the sitting is just data collection. For a Nad Al Hamar student with a 6.30pm weeknight slot, the practical pattern is to sit the paper at the weekend and use the weeknight session for the review.

sections.heading: What the in-home premium buys for a maths hour
paragraphs: A Nad Al Hamar family weighing an in-home maths tutor against an online one should see what the extra money is actually paying for. In-home one-to-one visits in Dubai are quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour once travel is absorbed, with Bestimate's rate table at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors asking AED 200 to 500. A qualified subject tutor teaching online is quoted at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, and IB specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270.

Break the in-home premium into its parts and it resolves into three things, none of which is teaching quality. The first is travel, paid for either in the rate or in a start time that slips. The second is scarcity: a tutor hireable within twenty minutes of an eastern residential district is drawn from a small pool, and small pools price upward regardless of quality. The third is convenience for the parent, which is a real benefit and should be priced honestly as one.

What it does not buy is the thing a maths problem actually needs, which is a person who has taught the specific course at the specific level and can discuss topic two and topic five by name. For Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level in Nad Al Hamar, that person probably does not live nearby. Paying a travel premium to hire from a pool that excludes them is paying more for less.

Against that, the genuine cases for an in-home arrangement should be acknowledged. A young child who cannot self-manage a screen. A student with a specific access need. A household with unreliable connectivity. None of those describes a Diploma mathematics student, who already works on a laptop daily. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE in any case; home tutoring is a service we run in India only, and if an adult in the room is the requirement, hire locally and ask to see the MoHRE private tuition work permit.

sections.heading: How a maths answer earns its marks, and what a tutor may not touch
paragraphs: Method marks are awarded for communicated reasoning, which means a correct answer with no visible working is worth less than a wrong answer with a correct method. Students resist this because it feels like being punished for being quick. The honest framing is that the examiner can only credit what is on the page, and a student who does three steps mentally and writes the fourth has asked to be marked on one line instead of four. Writing solutions out properly usually recovers several marks a paper and takes two sessions to establish as a habit.

Accuracy conventions carry marks of their own. Answers to three significant figures unless the question says otherwise, exact values where asked, units where the context has them, and no premature rounding inside a multi-step calculation. Each of these is one mark at a time, which is why students dismiss them, and together across a paper they are worth more than any single topic. A thirty-second check routine at the end of each question, practised until automatic, is the whole fix.

On the exploration, the boundary needs stating once rather than implied. A tutor may explain what each criterion rewards and in what proportion, screen a proposed topic for whether it can sustain mathematics at the level of the course, demonstrate a complete worked investigation on an entirely different topic, read the student's own draft and ask questions about assumptions, notation and depth, and say plainly that a section falls short of the level claimed. That is a substantial and legitimate service.

A tutor may not choose the topic, supply the mathematics, write or rewrite any passage, or edit the draft into shape. The exploration must be the student's own work, the school attests to it, and a malpractice finding falls on the candidate rather than on anyone else. At least one site ranking for these searches sells completed internal assessments outright. We do not, at any price, and the test of whether support was legitimate is whether the student can explain every line of their own work to their coordinator.
