sections.heading: What Diploma maths support costs, and what the island adds
paragraphs: Market figures belong here because the choice of format has a price attached. In-home one-to-one tuition in Dubai is quoted at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel included, with Bestimate's 2026 rate table putting the common range at AED 180 to AED 350 and independent home tutors advertising AED 200 to AED 500. Online qualified subject tutors are published at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors listing IB rates from AED 200 and TutorChase AED 270 for specialist work. Premium examiner-branded providers reach AED 500 to AED 650, with BartyED at AED 650. Those are market figures from the providers named, read in October 2026, and none is an IB Gram price list.

On a single-causeway island the in-home premium is substantially a travel premium. A tutor crossing Al Wasl Road at the end of the school day and queueing onto Pearl Jumeira spends thirty to fifty minutes each way, and that sits inside the rate. Nothing in it improves a session on integration by parts. Meanwhile the attribute that would improve it, experience of Higher Level Analysis and Approaches and of Paper 3, is not reliably signalled by price at all, because general and specialist maths tutors quote similar numbers in this market.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Pearl Jumeira families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with working annotated on a shared screen and kept, and recordings available. For mathematics the kept record matters more than in most subjects: a method line and a mark-scheme note from October are available in April, when the student is trying to recall precisely what earned the mark.

The second practical consequence is that adding the Higher Level second hour in the heavy term costs an hour rather than an hour plus two drives. That is what makes the two-hour arrangement affordable in the year it is actually needed, and it is the reason the planning advice on this page is possible to follow rather than merely sensible.

process.title: Settle the course and level with evidence
process.description: Before anything else, decide between Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, and between Standard and Higher Level, using marked IGCSE or MYP work and the stated requirements of plausible university courses. One session is usually enough, and it is the most consequential hour in the subject.

process.title: Claim the slot in September
process.description: We ask for school finish time and activity days before discussing mathematics, because the better window around 4:45pm is gone by January. A slot chosen around the week survives two years; one chosen around tutor availability collapses by the second term.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: A full session at no charge, taught rather than pitched, with the student. The tutor works from a recent marked paper and begins teaching. One trial lesson per student, before any booking is made; if the match is wrong, say so and nothing is owed.

process.title: Name the paper each hour targets
process.description: Paper 1 work is algebraic drill and exact values. Paper 2 work is problem setup and calculator technique. Paper 3 work is one long structured question end to end. Saying which at the start is the difference between teaching and general revision.

process.title: Reserve the exploration blocks early, then taper
process.description: Two longer sessions in the first year, one on whether the chosen topic contains enough mathematics and one on communication and reflection. In the final weeks the paid hours reduce deliberately, because accuracy and speed set through the student's own timed practice.

whyPoints.title: The course decision treated as the main event
whyPoints.description: Choosing between the two mathematics courses and between the two levels affects the grade more than any amount of weekly teaching. It is given a session of its own, worked from marked evidence and from course requirements checked at source rather than from a preference.

whyPoints.title: Matched on course, level and paper
whyPoints.description: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is among the tightest supply points in Dubai, because general maths experience transfers poorly to Paper 3 and to proof-style questions. Matching is done on that basis rather than on the word mathematics.

whyPoints.title: Method marks taught as a habit
whyPoints.description: The largest recoverable loss in Diploma mathematics is the method line a student does not write. It is a writing habit, it costs several marks a paper, and three weeks of insisting on it fixes it permanently. That work happens in the first month rather than in April.

whyPoints.title: Working that stays available
whyPoints.description: Annotated working and mark-scheme notes are kept on screen and recorded, so an exact-value technique shown in October can be reopened in April. For a subject where the convention matters as much as the answer, that record is worth more than a photograph of a whiteboard.

whyPoints.title: A second hour costs an hour
whyPoints.description: Higher Level usually needs two weekly hours in the second year, when vectors, integration, the exploration deadline and mocks arrive together. Because teaching is over live video, adding that hour costs an hour and nothing in travel across the causeway.

whyPoints.title: Honest limits on the exploration
whyPoints.description: A tutor explains the five criteria and their mark allocations, teaches the mathematics involved, tests whether a topic has enough mathematics in it, and gives feedback on the student's own draft. Nothing is written, redrafted or supplied, and no topic is handed over.

faqs.question: Which of the two IB maths courses fits a Pearl Jumeira student better?
faqs.answer: It depends on the student and on the courses they might apply for, in that order. Analysis and Approaches suits a student who is quick and accurate with algebra and tolerates abstraction, and it has a Paper 1 at both levels with no calculator permitted. Applications and Interpretation suits a student who reads data well and works in context, with technology permitted throughout and a heavier statistical load. It is not the easier course. Several competitive quantitative courses specify Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, so check requirements at source.

faqs.question: Is Applications and Interpretation seen as a weaker IB maths course?
faqs.answer: It is a different course rather than a weaker one, and treating it as a soft option causes problems in both directions. Students who take it expecting less work meet a substantial statistical load and an expectation of genuine calculator fluency as an assessed skill. Students who avoid it and struggle through Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level often end up with a materially worse grade than they would have achieved in the other route. The question to settle is which course the student will actually do well in.

faqs.question: What changes between Standard and Higher Level IB maths?
faqs.answer: Three things. Teaching time rises from 150 hours to 240. A third paper is added, worth 20 per cent, which is an extended structured problem unlike either of the first two. And the content deepens substantially, particularly in calculus, vectors and proof in Analysis and Approaches. The weightings also shift: Standard Level is two papers at 40 per cent each, Higher Level is three at 30, 30 and 20, with the exploration at 20 per cent in both. Level and course are separate decisions.

faqs.question: Why is Paper 3 the most neglected part of Higher Level maths?
faqs.answer: Because it does not resemble anything in the first two papers, and it is often met for the first time a few weeks before the examinations. It is worth 20 per cent of the Higher Level grade and consists of an extended investigation built up in stages, where an early error propagates through the remaining parts. The skill it rewards is persistence through a structured sequence, including carrying on with a stated assumption after a mistake. Two or three dedicated sessions in the second year is unusually high-value spending.

faqs.question: What is the biggest recoverable loss in IB maths papers?
faqs.answer: The method line that is never written. Diploma mark schemes award method marks for a correct approach even when the final answer is wrong, and students who work mentally or on a calculator and record only the answer forfeit them. It costs several marks a paper, it is a writing habit rather than a mathematical weakness, and roughly three weeks of being required to write the line fixes it permanently. No topic revision reaches those marks, which is why it is taught in the first month.

faqs.question: How much of the IB maths grade is the exploration, and how is it marked?
faqs.answer: Twenty per cent at both levels. It runs to roughly twelve to twenty pages and is marked against five criteria worth 20 marks between them: presentation at 4, mathematical communication at 4, personal engagement at 3, reflection at 3, and use of mathematics at 6. The largest single allocation is use of mathematics, which is why a beautifully written exploration about mathematics that is too simple cannot reach the upper bands. The topic choice in the first week usually decides the outcome.

faqs.question: What makes an exploration topic strong enough for the upper bands?
faqs.answer: Enough mathematics in it at the level of the course, and a genuine connection to the student. Use of mathematics carries the largest allocation, so content at the level of the first term will cap the mark regardless of how well it is written. Personal engagement is lost when a topic has been adopted rather than chosen, which is immediately visible to a reader. The useful test is whether the student can explain, unprompted, why they care about the question and what mathematics it will require.

faqs.question: Where is the line between exploration coaching and doing the work for a student?
faqs.answer: No, and the honest version of help is better described than it is sold. A tutor explains what each of the five criteria rewards and its mark allocation, teaches the mathematics the student has chosen to use, asks whether the topic contains enough mathematics to reach the upper bands, and gives feedback on a draft the student has written. Nothing is written, drafted, redrafted or supplied, and no topic is handed over. Submitting purchased work is a malpractice risk carried by the student alone.

faqs.question: What time should a maths session start for a Pearl Jumeira Diploma student?
faqs.answer: Around 4:45pm on an activity-free day, or from 6:45pm after food. School in this cluster ends between 2:45pm and 3:30pm, the causeway approach and drive home take thirty to forty-five minutes, and activity programmes run to about 6pm. Mathematics is the subject most sensitive to tiredness: a tired student still recognises question types and still makes arithmetic slips, which sends a tutor after the wrong problem. Nothing useful happens after about 8:30pm on a school night.

faqs.question: Does Higher Level maths need two sessions a week?
faqs.answer: Usually in the second year, and usually not in the first. The vectors and integration blocks arrive alongside the exploration deadline and the mock window, which is a predictable collision rather than a surprise. Two separate hours on different days allow work to be set, attempted alone and then marked, which a single longer block cannot because nothing has been attempted in between. Planning for the second hour in September costs the same as adding it in a panic and secures the better slot.

faqs.question: My child is losing physics marks. Is it actually a maths problem?
faqs.answer: Frequently, and the marked script will tell you within minutes. Diploma physics expects rearranging before substituting, confident standard form, trigonometry for resolving vectors, and gradient and area work on graphs, with some calculus at Higher Level. A student on Applications and Interpretation meets less of that incidentally. The diagnostic question is whether the error in the script is in the physics or in the algebra the physics required. If the maths is sound, a maths tutor is not the answer and anybody recommending one is selling hours.

faqs.question: Does IGCSE preparation differ depending on which IB maths course comes next?
faqs.answer: It does, and it is worth knowing in Year 10. Cambridge 0580 Extended, with its two-hour paper where no calculator is permitted, prepares a student for Analysis and Approaches Paper 1 better than Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 does, since Pearson permits a calculator in both of its papers. Several Dubai schools also set an Extended or Higher tier grade threshold for entry to Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, so IGCSE maths spending is partly spending to keep that route open.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a maths tutor to Pearl Jumeira?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE, since in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Pearl Jumeira families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with working annotated on a shared screen and kept afterwards. For mathematics that record is a real advantage: an exact-value technique or a mark-scheme note from October can be reopened in April, which is when a student is trying to recall precisely what earned the mark.

faqs.question: What do Higher Level maths tutors charge in Dubai, and does the island raise it?
faqs.answer: It raises in-home figures and not online ones. In-home one-to-one is quoted at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour including travel, with Bestimate's 2026 table putting the common range at AED 180 to AED 350. Online qualified subject tutors are published at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors listing IB from AED 200 and TutorChase AED 270. Premium providers reach AED 650, with BartyED at that figure. On a single-causeway island much of the in-home premium covers the approach rather than the teaching.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-pearl-jumeira.closingHeading: Settle the course, claim the slot, name the paper
dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-pearl-jumeira.closingBody: Three decisions carry Diploma mathematics for a Pearl Jumeira family, and only one of them is about a tutor. Decide between Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, and between the two levels, from marked evidence and from course requirements checked on the universities' own pages. Claim the better afternoon slot in September, because it is gone by January. Then insist that each hour names the paper it targets, so the time goes on algebraic drill, problem setup or an extended structured question rather than on maths in general. Take the free trial lesson first; teaching is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-remraam.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches and Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation at both levels. Each profile names route and level, because the two courses carry different topic lists and different papers and should never be treated as one subject.

intro.heading: Maths rewards the week, not the term
paragraphs: Mathematics is the Diploma subject most sensitive to how work is distributed. Thirty minutes four times a week beats two hours once, by a margin large enough to change a grade, because fluency decays and retrieval strengthens with spacing. Nearly every student in this corridor does the opposite: nothing for a fortnight, then a long session before an assessment, and the fluency never accumulates.

That makes the useful unit of planning the week rather than the term. A maths week needs four things in it: a short retrieval block on material from a month ago, a short non-calculator block, work on the current topic, and one timed section. None of those takes long. All four are usually missing, and adding them is the single highest-return change available before any tutoring is bought.

Remraam shapes the week in practice. It is a low-rise apartment community in Dubailand, built as the Al Thamam and Al Ramth clusters with its own park and retail, reached from Al Qudra Road and Emirates Road. South View School sits close by and takes students through Year 11, so Diploma students have usually moved outward to Dubai Hills, Al Barsha South or The Sustainable City, and their afternoons are longer than they were a year earlier.

The second thing this page sets out is topic order. Most students meet Diploma mathematics in the sequence the school teaches it, which is reasonable for a class and sometimes wrong for an individual. A student with weak algebraic foundations who meets calculus on schedule will fail at calculus for algebraic reasons, and the fix is to move the foundation work forward rather than to repeat the calculus.

A third element is technology, and it is handled badly in both directions. Analysis students use a calculator for everything and then meet a paper taken without one. Applications students own a graphing calculator whose statistics menus and solvers they have never explored, and lose marks to slow use in a paper where speed is part of the test. Both are timeline problems rather than ability problems: the work belongs in the first term of Year 12, when there is no pressure attached, and almost nobody does it then.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time, so a session can sit at a quarter past four or after eight depending on the household. Home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only, and nothing here should be read as an offer to arrive at an Al Thamam or Al Ramth address. The dates that genuinely matter appear in the final table, and IB session dates are not among them because they belong to the school's coordinator. Everything below is organised around those three ideas: the week, the topic order, and the technology.

sections.heading: How to build a maths week
paragraphs: A maths week has four jobs and most students do one of them. The first is retrieval: ten or fifteen minutes on material from three or four weeks ago, with no notes, specifically to make old topics come back under cold conditions. Without it a student knows everything they studied recently and little from the first term, which is exactly the wrong shape for a terminal examination.

The second is non-calculator work, which in Analysis and Approaches is not optional and in Applications still matters for mental estimation. Short sets, fifteen minutes, marked immediately, with each error labelled as either a slip or a method failure. Those two need completely different responses and students lump them together as being careless, which is not a diagnosis.

The third is the current topic from school, which is the only one most students do, usually as whatever homework was set. The fourth is one timed section a week from a real past paper of the student's own route and level. Not a full paper, which is too large to sustain weekly, but twenty-five minutes against a clock, which keeps the pacing habit alive all year rather than only in the final term.

Four blocks, roughly ninety minutes of work across the week outside school homework. That is a realistic ask even from a long Remraam afternoon, and it is more valuable than a two-hour session once a fortnight. The tutoring session's main job in this model is not to teach for an hour; it is to check the four blocks, fix what they exposed, and set the next week.

sections.heading: Topic order across two years, and when to break it
paragraphs: Schools teach Diploma mathematics in a sequence that works for a class, and for most students following it is correct. It stops being correct where a student's foundation is uneven, because topics in mathematics are not independent and a weakness underneath surfaces as failure above.

The commonest example is algebraic manipulation. A student who cannot rearrange reliably, handle indices and surds, or work with functions as objects will fail at calculus, and the failure looks like calculus. Repeating the calculus does nothing. Moving the algebra forward, as its own short block for three or four weeks, fixes both. The same pattern applies with logarithms arriving late and blocking exponential models, and with trigonometric identities blocking later integration.

In Applications and Interpretation the equivalent is statistical literacy: a student who does not really understand what a correlation coefficient is cannot interpret a regression, and will produce correct computation with meaningless commentary. That has to be addressed before the modelling content rather than during it.

The practical approach is to look at the school's scheme of work for the next term, identify what each upcoming topic assumes, and test those assumptions early. That is a thirty-minute exercise for a tutor with the scheme in hand, and it reorders the next two months of work more usefully than any amount of revision.

There is a limit to how far this should be pushed. A student cannot be taught a parallel course, and falling behind the class creates its own problems in a subject where lessons build on each other. The right scale is three or four weeks of foundation work running alongside the school's teaching, not a reordering of the whole year, and it should be agreed with the student so that the point of it is clear rather than feeling like a demotion.

sections.heading: The technology timeline
paragraphs: Technology is handled badly in most maths plans, in both directions. Students in Analysis and Approaches use a calculator for everything until a mock reveals that the first paper is taken without one. Students in Applications and Interpretation own a graphing calculator whose capabilities they have never explored, and lose marks to slow or clumsy use in a paper where speed matters.

The sensible sequence starts early. In the first term of Year 12, establish which paper in the student's route is non-calculator and begin the weekly non-calculator block immediately, when there is no pressure attached. In the same term, make the student learn their own calculator model properly: statistics menus, graph intersections, solvers, stored values. A session on the machine itself is not a waste of money; it is a paper's worth of time saved.

Through Year 13 the two streams run in parallel and the discipline is keeping them apart. Non-calculator practice has to be genuinely non-calculator, which means the machine off the desk rather than face down. Calculator practice should include a written plan line before any use, so the technology confirms reasoning instead of searching for an answer.

In the final weeks the technology work becomes logistics: mode settings checked, memory cleared according to the school's instructions, batteries replaced, a spare available if permitted. Those are small things that occasionally cost a paper, and they belong on a checklist rather than in anyone's memory.

One school-specific point to check. Schools differ in what they tell students about clearing calculator memory and about which models are permitted, and those instructions come from the examination centre rather than from a tutor. Ask the department for them in writing in the term before the papers, and put them on the same checklist as everything else.

sections.heading: Decision points, with the dates that matter
paragraphs: A handful of decisions set the ceiling of a Diploma maths grade, and all of them arrive before a family feels urgency. Naming them with their timing is more useful than any amount of general advice, because each has a window that closes.

The route and level decision happens late in Year 11, on the strength of IGCSE or Middle Years work, and it determines both the content and the university doors that stay open. The exploration topic is approved early in Year 12, and a topic without accessible mathematics cannot be rescued by effort afterwards. A level change between Higher and Standard is easier early in Year 12 than late, and in some schools becomes impossible once the second year begins because teaching groups diverge.

Then come the fixed points: the school's own exploration draft and submission dates, the autumn mock in Year 13 that feeds predicted grades, and the session itself. The school sets the first two, which means they differ between the Dubai schools students from this community attend and cannot be looked up in a general guide.

IB session and results dates are deliberately absent from this page. The IB's own site, through the school's Diploma coordinator, is the only reliable source, and a tutoring page that restates them for search traffic is wrong within a year while parents act on it. What is safe to plan against is the sequence, and the sequence does not move.

sections.heading: The exploration, and why topic choice is the whole game
paragraphs: The exploration carries roughly a fifth of the maths grade and is the only part of it a family can still influence mid-course, which makes it the most improvable component available. It is a piece of personal mathematical writing rather than a long report, and schools publish the current page guidance from the subject guide.

Its criteria cover presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics. Students put their effort into the last of those and lose marks across the first four, which are credited separately. A reflection naming a limitation in a model and considering what relaxing an assumption would do scores properly; one saying the topic was interesting does not. That is a writing skill and it is teachable quickly.

Topic choice sets the ceiling before a word is written. The test is whether the student can say in one sentence what mathematics they will do and why they personally chose this. A topic that sounds impressive but contains no mathematics at the student's level cannot be rescued by work, and one so broad that the mathematics becomes a survey cannot demonstrate engagement. Both failures happen at approval, which is precisely when help is cheapest.

The boundary is strict and worth stating. A tutor explains criteria, questions the topic, critiques the mathematics and marks the student's own draft against descriptors. A tutor does not draft, rewrite, edit to completion or supply a worked exploration to adapt. The work is authenticated by the teacher, and an authenticity finding can cost the Diploma rather than marks.

sections.heading: Ramadan, travel and holding a weekly structure
paragraphs: A weekly structure is only useful if it survives the year, and the UAE calendar interrupts it in predictable ways. Ramadan shortens school days and shifts energy patterns, long breaks remove the school scaffolding entirely, and families along this corridor travel for several weeks at a time.

Ramadan is the easiest to handle. Because the lesson arrives over live video with nobody driving, a slot can move after Iftar at no cost and be rearranged week by week. The four weekly blocks shrink rather than stop: retrieval and non-calculator work are short enough to survive a reduced day, and the timed section moves to a weekend. Keeping something going matters more than keeping the full volume.

Breaks are the opposite problem. Without school homework the current-topic block disappears and most students do nothing at all, which is why fluency frequently drops across a long holiday and has to be rebuilt in the first weeks of term. A reduced version of the week, perhaps two blocks rather than four, protects most of it. Breaks are also the only time three or four sessions in a week is realistic, which makes them the natural slot for an exploration push.

Travel should be declared when the plan is made rather than discovered later. A block sized to the weeks that actually exist works; one sized to a theoretical term collapses, and the collapse is usually blamed on the student.

There is also a case for deliberately stopping. A week before the papers, and during the examination fortnight itself, additional input usually helps less than rest does, and a student who revises hard in that window arrives tired. Tiredness costs more marks in a non-calculator paper than any remaining content gap, which makes the decision to stop a plan rather than a failure of discipline.

sections.heading: What a maths plan costs, priced as blocks
paragraphs: Because the weekly structure does most of the work, the sensible spend is lower and more intermittent than families expect. One session a week through Year 12 to set and check the week, a short twice-weekly block in the heavy autumn of Year 13, an exploration push of three or four sessions, and a final-stretch block. That is considerably less than a continuous weekly hour for two years and tends to produce more.

The bands are published and checkable. A qualified subject tutor working online in Dubai sits at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200 and IGCSE from AED 150. Subject specialists run AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and Bestimate's Dubai cost table giving AED 200 to 450 or more, while premium examiner-led provision reaches AED 650 at BartyED.

The cheaper tier has a legitimate role in this model. Budget online and university-student tutors advertise from around AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya AED 33 to 52, and marking a student's weekly blocks is work that tier can often do well. In-home visits are quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 with travel folded in, Bestimate at AED 180 to 350 and home tutors at AED 200 to 500.

Monthly, Bestimate's estimates for a weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. For household context, KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for 2026-27. These are market figures with their sources named, not IB Gram prices.

sections.heading: Permits, boundaries and what to ask a maths tutor
paragraphs: An individual giving private lessons in the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. It covers registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18, and MoHRE's service listing shows no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Tutoring without it attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published.

A tutoring business with premises in Dubai needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute instead, renewed annually with the request made at least 30 days before expiry. IB Gram has no UAE premises, holds no such permit, and does not attach a regulator's name to its tutors. One arrangement to decline outright: Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct carries a similar bar.

On materials, IB subject guides, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to their publishers. Sessions reference the official pages and link out rather than circulating copies, and nobody holds unreleased material whatever is implied about examiner connections.

The questions worth asking a maths tutor are narrow and answerable. Which route and level have you taught, and for how many cohorts. How do you structure a student's week. How do you drill non-calculator work. What will you refuse to do with an exploration draft. Four answers, and the choice tends to make itself.

process.title: Name the route, level and school
process.description: Analysis at Higher Level and Applications at Standard Level are different courses with different papers and topic lists. Naming the school as well tells us the topic order, the exploration deadline and the mock window the plan has to respect.

process.title: Describe the current week honestly
process.description: What maths actually happens between lessons now, including if the answer is only school homework. The first thing a plan changes is usually the week rather than the knowledge, and that cannot be designed without knowing where it starts.

process.title: Send one marked paper
process.description: A marked mock or past paper separates slips from method failures, timing collapse from misreading, and technique from genuine content absence. Those have repair times from a fortnight to several months, and only the script distinguishes them.

process.title: Free trial lesson, then four blocks set
process.description: A trial over live video at no cost and before payment. If it goes ahead, the first session's output is a week the student can run alone: a retrieval set, a non-calculator set, current-topic work and one timed section.

process.title: Review the blocks, not the feeling
process.description: Each session starts by marking what the four blocks produced, which makes progress visible and keeps the conversation factual. Every four to six weeks the plan is checked against the exploration deadline and the mock window.

whyPoints.title: The week is designed, not just the hour
whyPoints.description: Mathematics responds to distributed practice more than any other Diploma subject. Four short blocks across the week outside school homework is worth more than a long session once a fortnight, and the session's job is to set and check them.

whyPoints.title: Topic order is tested against the student
whyPoints.description: A school's sequence suits a class. Where a student's algebra is shaky, meeting calculus on schedule produces failure that looks like calculus. Testing what each upcoming topic assumes reorders the next two months more usefully than revision does.

whyPoints.title: Non-calculator work starts in the first term
whyPoints.description: Fluency for the non-calculator paper degrades silently, because school classwork almost always has technology to hand. A weekly fifteen-minute set started early costs nothing and prevents a discovery in the autumn mock of Year 13.

whyPoints.title: The exploration is treated as the live component
whyPoints.description: It carries roughly a fifth of the grade and its deadline is still movable, and both of its common failures happen at topic approval. One session then is worth several spent polishing prose a year later.

whyPoints.title: Blocks are intermittent and end on a date
whyPoints.description: A continuous weekly hour for twenty-four months costs more than the four blocks this page recommends and delivers less. Every arrangement proposed here carries a length and a purpose, including the ones we advise stopping.

whyPoints.title: No invented dates and no regulator claims
whyPoints.description: No IB session or results date appears here, because the school's coordinator is the only reliable source. IB Gram holds no KHDA permit, no ADEK registration and no board affiliation, and will not use a regulator's name as a credential.

faqs.question: How much maths should happen between weekly sessions?
faqs.answer: About ninety minutes across the week, split into four short blocks outside school homework. Ten to fifteen minutes of cold retrieval on material from three or four weeks ago, fifteen minutes of non-calculator work marked immediately, the current topic from school, and one twenty-five minute timed section from a real past paper. Mathematics responds to distributed practice far more than to long single sessions, and most students in this corridor do only the third block. Adding the other three is the highest-return change available before any tutoring is bought.

faqs.question: Why does our daughter forget topics from the first term?
faqs.answer: Because nothing in a normal week asks her to retrieve them. School homework follows the current topic, so material from two months ago is never tested until a mock, and by then it feels unlearned rather than unpractised. The fix is a short weekly retrieval block with no notes available, deliberately on old material. It is uncomfortable for a fortnight and then it works, and it is the cheapest intervention on this page because it requires no teaching at all.

faqs.question: Should a Remraam student follow the school's topic order exactly?
faqs.answer: Usually, and not always. A school's sequence is designed for a class and is sensible for most students. It stops being sensible where a foundation is uneven, because mathematics topics are not independent: a student who cannot rearrange reliably or handle indices and surds will fail at calculus for algebraic reasons, and repeating the calculus changes nothing. Looking at the next term's scheme of work, identifying what each topic silently assumes, and testing those assumptions early reorders the coming months more usefully than revision does.

faqs.question: When should non-calculator practice begin for Analysis and Approaches?
faqs.answer: In the first term of Year 12, before there is any pressure attached. The first paper in that route is taken without a calculator, while school classwork and homework almost always have technology to hand, so the fluency degrades without anyone noticing and is discovered in a mock. Fifteen minutes a week, short sets marked immediately with every error labelled as either a slip or a method failure, is enough. Those two categories need different responses, and students lump them together as carelessness, which is not a diagnosis.

faqs.question: Is a session on the calculator itself worth paying for?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and it surprises people. Most students in Applications and Interpretation own a graphing calculator whose statistics menus, intersection tools, solvers and stored-value functions they have never properly explored, and lose marks to slow or clumsy use in a paper where speed matters. One session on the machine can save a paper's worth of time. The companion habit is writing a plan line before any calculator use, so the technology confirms reasoning rather than searching for an answer the student has not reasoned towards.

faqs.question: What are the decision points that set a maths grade ceiling?
faqs.answer: Four, and all arrive before families feel urgency. The route and level choice late in Year 11 determines both content and which university doors stay open. A level change between Higher and Standard is practical early in Year 12 and often impossible later, because teaching groups diverge. The exploration topic is approved early in Year 12, and a topic without accessible mathematics cannot be rescued afterwards. Then the school's own exploration deadlines and the autumn mock, both set internally and therefore different between schools.

faqs.question: How long should the exploration actually be?
faqs.answer: It is a piece of personal mathematical writing rather than a long report, and schools publish the current page guidance from the subject guide, which is the figure to work from. Length matters less than people assume. What scores is a focused question, correct and clearly communicated mathematics, genuine personal engagement, and reflection that names a limitation in a model and considers what relaxing an assumption would change. Three of the five criteria are not about the mathematics itself, and that is where most marks are left.

faqs.question: Can a tutor suggest an exploration topic?
faqs.answer: A tutor can question topics the student proposes, explain why one will not support enough mathematics, and point at the kinds of question that tend to work. What a tutor should not do is hand over a topic for the student to execute, because personal engagement is a graded criterion and a borrowed topic is visible in the writing. The useful test the student has to pass themselves is saying in one sentence what mathematics they will do and why they chose it. If they cannot, the topic is not ready.

faqs.question: How does the week change during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: It shrinks rather than stops. School days shorten and energy patterns shift, so the retrieval and non-calculator blocks continue because they are short, the current-topic work follows whatever school sets, and the timed section moves to a weekend. Sessions themselves commonly move to after Iftar, which costs nothing to arrange because the lesson arrives over live video and nobody is driving to Al Thamam or Al Ramth. Keeping something going matters considerably more than keeping the full volume.

faqs.question: What happens to fluency over a long school holiday?
faqs.answer: It drops, reliably, and then the first weeks of term are spent rebuilding it instead of moving forward. The cause is structural: without school homework the current-topic block vanishes and most students do nothing at all. Keeping two of the four blocks going, retrieval and non-calculator work, protects most of it for about twenty minutes a day. Breaks are also the only period when three or four sessions in a week is realistic, which makes them the natural window for an exploration push.

faqs.question: Is Applications and Interpretation a safer choice than Analysis?
faqs.answer: Different rather than safer. Applications assumes technology throughout and is built on modelling and statistics; at Higher Level it carries matrices, graph theory and complex numbers plus a modelling investigation that defeats students who chose it to avoid calculus. Analysis is harder on manipulation and proof and has a non-calculator paper. The real constraint is usually university entry: engineering, physics and many mathematics courses expect Analysis, often at Higher Level, and those requirements should be read from each institution's own published entry profile.

faqs.question: How many sessions does this weekly model actually need?
faqs.answer: Fewer than a continuous arrangement. One session a week through Year 12 whose job is setting and checking the four blocks, a short twice-weekly block through the heavy autumn of Year 13, three or four sessions for the exploration, and a final-stretch block of eight to twelve weeks. Priced at the qualified online band of roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, that totals less than a weekly hour sustained for two years and generally produces more.

faqs.question: Can a cheaper tutor mark the weekly blocks?
faqs.answer: Often, and it is a sensible use of that tier. Budget online and university-student tutors advertise from roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour in this market, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya AED 33 to 52, and marking a student's retrieval and non-calculator sets against answers is work that can be done well at that price. What the cheaper tier rarely provides is the diagnosis: deciding from a marked paper which topics to reorder and whether a loss is a slip or a method failure.

faqs.question: Does the step from IGCSE maths need separate work before Year 12?
faqs.answer: Usually, and the summer is the moment. The jump is mostly about fluency and independence rather than new ideas: a student who reached a strong IGCSE grade with a calculator always to hand meets a non-calculator paper and a pace that assumes manipulation is automatic. Students from this community generally sat IGCSE locally at South View School and then moved, so they arrive in a Diploma class alongside students from several boards. Six to eight sessions across the break on manipulation, exact values and notation makes the first term ordinary.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-remraam.closingBody: The useful first message from Remraam says the route, the level, the school, and honestly what maths currently happens between lessons. Attach one marked paper and a free trial lesson over live video is arranged before any payment is taken. What comes out of it should be four short weekly blocks the student can run alone, with the session's job being to check them and set the next week. Lessons are delivered online on Gulf Standard Time; home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-serena.tutorsIntro: The maths specialists matched to Serena families name the course and the paper before anything else. The free first lesson is spent on two marked papers, because that is where the losses are visible rather than in a conversation about difficult topics.

intro.heading: The honest answer: which of the four courses is it?
paragraphs: Serena is a townhouse community off Al Qudra Road at the outer edge of the Dubailand belt, among clusters including Bella Casa and Casa Viva, with Mudon, Villanova and Remraam alongside. Its Diploma students travel to a handful of IB schools across the city, which means a parent asking whether anyone nearby knows the syllabus is asking a question geography cannot settle. What settles it is whether the tutor can name the course.

There are four. Analysis and Approaches is the proof-and-calculus route; Applications and Interpretation is the statistics-and-modelling route. Each runs at Higher and Standard Level. They differ in content, in paper structure, in whether a graphing calculator is allowed, and in the command terms that appear most often. A tutor who treats them as one subject with four difficulty settings will teach the wrong habits confidently.

The mistake is not theoretical. We regularly see Applications and Interpretation students who have been drilled on non-calculator algebraic manipulation, which is an Analysis and Approaches Standard Level skill and appears in no Applications paper. We see Analysis and Approaches Higher Level students who have never attempted a Paper 3 question, which is sixty minutes and 20 per cent of their grade. Both are the result of a tutor teaching a subject rather than a course.

IB Gram matches a student to a tutor who teaches their named course and the paper that is going wrong, and teaches live online, one-to-one, on Gulf Standard Time. No tutor travels to a UAE address, because home visits are a service we run only in India, and there is no IB Gram office or centre in the country. The trade is that the pool is selected on course knowledge rather than on willingness to drive to Al Qudra Road.

What follows is the detail that lets you interrogate any maths tutor. The question set that identifies real course knowledge. Which topics appear on which paper. The calculator rules, paper by paper. The command terms that decide marks — show that, hence, deduce, justify, verify. The Exploration timeline counted backwards from a school deadline. What actually separates a 5 from a 7. And when switching course or level mid-course is still possible.

Two standing notes. We publish no IB exam or results dates, because ibo.org blocks automated verification and a date a family plans around has to be checkable; ask your child's IB coordinator. And subject guides are revised, so confirm paper durations and weightings for your child's cohort with the school rather than treating any page as final, including this one. What does not change between guides is the structure of the problem: a named course, a set of papers with specific calculator rules, a set of command terms that mean specific things, and an Exploration whose ceiling is decided by its topic.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-serena.programmesIntro: Maths support requests from this community arrive at three predictable moments, and the right response differs at each.

programmes.name: MYP Mathematics, standard and extended
programmes.description: Four criteria, each marked 0 to 8: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Criterion B is the one students lose, because generalising a pattern and justifying it is a different skill from calculating correctly and is rarely taught directly. The extended strand is the realistic entry route to Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level.
programmes.countryNote: MYP provision in the Dubailand belt is thinner than Diploma provision, so Serena students on this track often travel further. The investigation tasks that carry Criterion B need uninterrupted thinking time, which makes them the work most worth protecting an early slot or a weekend morning for.

programmes.name: Diploma year one
programmes.description: The year the course choice becomes real and the Exploration begins. Most useful work here is foundational: algebraic fluency for Analysis and Approaches, statistical process discipline for Applications and Interpretation, and at Higher Level an early introduction to Paper 3 so that the first encounter is not in a mock.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai schools the Exploration deadline generally falls weeks before the IB's own date, and typically in the same window as two or three other internal assessments. Planning backwards from the school's calendar rather than the IB's is the single most useful scheduling decision available in DP1.

programmes.name: Diploma year two
programmes.description: Content finishes, mocks arrive, and the grade is decided by whether knowledge converts into marks. Sessions here are past-paper driven: timed questions marked to the mark scheme, with every lost mark categorised as content, method or command-term misreading. Paper 3 gets its own allocation at Higher Level rather than being squeezed in.
programmes.countryNote: UAE schools sit the May session. We publish no IB dates because they cannot be verified from ibo.org, so the planning anchors are the school's mock week and its internal deadlines. Ask the IB coordinator for both in writing at the start of DP2.

programmes.name: What the course choice decides
programmes.description: Engineering, physics, mathematics and many economics programmes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, frequently at Higher Level. Applications and Interpretation is accepted widely for business, social sciences, design and several life-science routes. The constraint is real and it is set two years earlier, which is why the route decision deserves evidence rather than preference.
programmes.countryNote: Requirements vary by university and by individual programme, so read the specific programme pages for the institutions your child is considering. For Ministry of Education equivalency the British-track rules are published while no IB points threshold has been read on moe.gov.ae, so verify any IB equivalency question with the Ministry.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-serena.subjectsIntro: This page is about maths, so these are the components and topic strands, with the paper each belongs to and the specific habit that costs marks.

subjects.name: Algebra and functions
subjects.description: Transformations, composite and inverse functions, logarithms and exponentials. Transformations are the most mis-taught topic in this market: learned as memorised shift rules rather than as operations on a function's input and output, which fails the moment two combine.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.levels: AA HL and SL; AI in applied form
subjects.description: Differentiation and integration with their applications. The reliable loss is the chain rule inside a product or quotient, and integration by substitution where the substitution is not signposted. Both are fluency problems rather than comprehension problems.

subjects.name: Trigonometry
subjects.description: Radians, identities and equations, with compound-angle work at Higher Level. Equations with multiple solutions in a stated interval are the classic loss: the student finds one solution and stops, which a required sketch prevents almost entirely.

subjects.name: Proof
subjects.description: Direct proof, proof by induction and, at Higher Level, contradiction. Appears on the non-calculator paper and rewards structure: a correct conclusion without the inductive step stated earns little. Highly teachable in a small number of sessions because the structures are fixed.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.levels: AI HL and SL; AA core
subjects.description: In Applications and Interpretation this is the heart of the course: hypothesis testing, chi-squared, regression and distributions. Marks go missing in process rather than calculation — hypotheses unstated, p-value not compared to the significance level, conclusion not written in context.

subjects.name: Matrices and graph theory
subjects.description: Part of the Higher Level breadth that students choosing Applications and Interpretation for an easier life do not expect. Self-contained and learnable, but it arrives in DP1 and is frequently postponed until it collides with the Exploration.

subjects.name: Paper 1
subjects.description: Short and extended response. In Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level it is sat without a graphing calculator, which is the single biggest difference across the suite. In Applications and Interpretation a calculator is permitted, and the examinable habit is showing the input.

subjects.name: Paper 2
subjects.description: Calculator permitted in every course. The failure mode is an answer transcribed from a display with no visible method, which forfeits process marks the student had earned mentally. Knowing which questions are faster by hand is worth several marks.

subjects.name: Paper 3
subjects.description: Sixty minutes, 20 per cent of the grade, two extended-response investigations built through scaffolded parts. It tests sustained reasoning rather than recall, which is why more Paper 1 practice does not prepare anyone for it. Needs its own stream in any plan.

subjects.name: The Mathematical Exploration
subjects.description: Independent mathematical writing worth 20 per cent, marked on five criteria totalling 20 marks. Criterion E, use of mathematics, carries six of them and decides the ceiling, so topic viability must be tested before the student invests weeks.

subjects.name: Graphing calculator technique
subjects.levels: Every paper except AA SL Paper 1
subjects.description: An examinable skill, not an aid. Marks go to students who state the input, sketch what the display showed and name the test used. Twenty minutes of deliberate calculator training is often worth more than an hour of content revision.

subjects.name: Command terms
subjects.description: Show that, hence, deduce, justify, verify and write down each demand something specific. 'Hence' requires using the previous result; 'write down' signals that no working is expected and none should be shown. Misreading them costs marks before the mathematics is examined.

sections.heading: The questions that identify real course knowledge
paragraphs: Ask these four and you will know within two minutes whether a tutor teaches the course or the subject. They work equally well on a neighbour's recommendation, an agency and us.

Which of the four courses is my child on, and what does the level add? A tutor who teaches it will say that Higher Level in either route adds Paper 3, sixty minutes and 20 per cent of the grade, and will say what Paper 3 is like. Which papers permit a graphing calculator? The correct answer names Analysis and Approaches Standard Level Paper 1 as the exception across the whole suite, and that detail alone separates the informed from the confident.

What is Criterion E worth on the Exploration, and what does it reward? Six of twenty marks, for the relevance, accuracy and sophistication of the mathematics used, which is why topic choice sets the ceiling. And finally: what does 'hence' require in a question? A tutor who teaches the course will answer that it obliges the student to use the previous result, and that ignoring it loses marks even when the final answer is right.

None of these are trick questions and none of them are about years of experience. They are about whether somebody has taught this course, under the current guide, through a cycle. In a belt where IB provision is thin and students travel across the city to a handful of schools, those people are not concentrated near Al Qudra Road — which is the honest answer to the proximity question.

sections.heading: Which topics appear on which paper
paragraphs: Students revise topics; examiners set papers. The mapping between the two is where a lot of wasted revision happens, and it is rarely explained. A student who knows which paper a topic is likely to appear on, and in what form, revises differently and better.

The broad pattern is that Paper 1 and Paper 2 both sample across the syllabus, with the distinguishing factor being calculator access rather than content. Proof, algebraic manipulation and exact-value work cluster where no calculator is permitted. Statistical tests, regression and anything requiring numerical solution cluster where one is. Paper 3, at Higher Level, is different in kind: two extended investigations that build through parts and can draw on anything.

The table below sets out the practical consequences for revision. The column that matters most is the last one, because it names the form a topic takes rather than the topic itself. 'Revise trigonometry' is not a plan. 'Practise trigonometric equations with multiple solutions in a stated interval, sketching first' is a plan, and it takes an hour rather than a week.

One caution: paper structures and weightings are revised between subject guides, so confirm the current arrangement for your child's cohort with the school. What does not change is the principle that revision should be organised by paper and question form rather than by chapter order, which is how most students revise and why so much of it does not show up in marks.

sections.heading: Calculator rules, paper by paper
paragraphs: This is the detail that most distinguishes the four courses in practice, and the one most often got wrong by a tutor teaching from general mathematical competence. The rule is simple and its consequences are not.

Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level sits Paper 1 without a graphing calculator. That is the only paper in the entire suite where a student must work by hand throughout, and it is where students who have leaned on technology quietly fall apart: surds, logarithm laws, exact trigonometric values and algebraic fractions all have to be fluent. At Higher Level, Analysis and Approaches also sits a paper without a calculator, with the same consequence at greater depth.

Applications and Interpretation permits a graphing calculator throughout. The examined habit is therefore completely different: stating the input used, sketching what the display showed, naming the statistical test, and interpreting output rather than producing it. A student drilled on non-calculator manipulation for this course has been prepared for an examination they will not sit.

The teaching consequence is that calculator work is a syllabus item rather than a convenience. Twenty minutes spent on deliberate calculator technique — windows that hide roots, storing values rather than retyping rounded ones, showing the input in the answer — regularly recovers more marks than an hour of content revision. Confirm your child's paper arrangement against the current guide, since structures are revised, and make sure the physical calculator is in the room during sessions rather than an emulator.

sections.heading: Command terms: the cheapest marks in the subject
paragraphs: Maths command terms are specific instructions, and students treat them as stylistic variation. That misreading costs marks before any mathematics is assessed, and it is the fastest thing a competent tutor fixes.

'Show that' means the answer is given and the working is the mark: a student who writes the given answer with no derivation earns nothing. 'Hence' obliges the use of the previous result, so a correct answer obtained independently can lose marks. 'Write down' signals that no working is expected, which means time spent producing it is wasted. 'Deduce' expects a conclusion drawn from a stated result rather than a fresh calculation. 'Justify' requires a reason, not an assertion. 'Verify' means substitute and confirm, not solve from scratch.

Each of those is worth marks in both papers of every course, and together they are the highest-yield hour available in IB maths. A single session in which a student marks their own last paper against the command terms typically reveals four to eight marks lost to misreading alone, which at Standard Level can be the difference between grade boundaries.

It is also the clearest test of a tutor. Ask what 'hence' requires. Somebody who has taught the course answers immediately; somebody who has taught mathematics in general will explain that it means 'therefore', which is true in English and insufficient in an examination. The command terms are published in the subject guide, which is the document any serious tutor works from and which should be cited rather than reproduced.

'Hence': the previous result must be used, even if another route works
'Write down': no working expected, so producing it wastes time

sections.heading: The Exploration, counted backwards from the school's deadline
paragraphs: The Mathematical Exploration is 20 per cent of the grade in all four courses and is marked on five criteria totalling twenty marks: presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics. Criterion E, use of mathematics, carries six marks and sets the ceiling, because it assesses whether the mathematics is relevant, correct and sophisticated enough for the level.

That single fact determines the timeline. A topic with too little real mathematics in it cannot score on E however well the piece is written, so viability has to be tested before any work begins. Twenty minutes with a tutor or a willing teacher at that stage protects a fifth of the subject grade; the same conversation after the data is gathered protects nothing.

Working backwards from the school's internal deadline rather than the IB's — the school's is earlier and is the one that bites — the sequence below is what a calm Exploration looks like. It is not demanding; it simply has to start earlier than most students start. The commonest version of this component in Dubai schools is a topic chosen late, mathematics that turns out to be thin, and a frantic fortnight producing presentation on an already-capped piece.

The boundary is firm. A tutor may test the topic's viability, explain each criterion, question reasoning and comment on a draft the student wrote. A tutor may not choose the topic and hand it over, write or rewrite text, produce or process data, or supply a past student's Exploration as a model. Those are passing off another person's work as the student's own, which risks the Diploma rather than one grade.

sections.heading: What actually separates a 5 from a 7
paragraphs: Parents ask what it takes to move a grade, and in maths the answer is unusually concrete because the losses are visible on paper. Between a 5 and a 7 the difference is rarely a missing topic.

At the 5 level, students typically know the content and lose marks in volume to four things: method not shown, command terms misread, calculator answers given without input or interpretation, and questions abandoned when a step fails. All four are habits, all four are visible in a marked paper, and all four close in a small number of sessions with strict marking rather than more teaching.

Reaching a 7 requires something different: fluency under time pressure, and the ability to sustain reasoning across an extended question. That is why Paper 3 is the Higher Level differentiator — it cannot be passed by recognition, only by reasoning — and why timed practice matters more at the top than content coverage does. A student who can do every question given unlimited time and scores a 5 has a pace problem, not a knowledge problem.

The practical conclusion is a two-stage plan rather than a single arrangement. Stage one: strict marking of past work until the four habit losses stop appearing, which is usually four to six sessions. Stage two: timed work, extended questions and, at Higher Level, Paper 3 reasoning, which is a longer-running commitment. Families who buy stage two first spend more and move less, because the habit losses continue underneath the harder work.

sections.heading: Switching course or level mid-Diploma
paragraphs: A recurring question from this belt, usually in the first term of DP1: my child is in the wrong maths course, can they move? The answer is school-dependent and time-sensitive, and worth asking early rather than hoping it resolves.

The school owns the decision, because it holds the assessment record, the timetable and the registration. Practically, movement is easiest early in DP1 and becomes progressively harder as the course proceeds, both because content diverges and because registration deadlines approach. A move from Higher to Standard Level within the same route is usually simpler than a move between Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, which are different courses rather than different levels.

What a tutor can usefully contribute is evidence rather than advocacy. Two marked papers and a short diagnostic conversation will usually show whether the difficulty is the course or the preparation. A student losing marks on method, command terms and timing is in the right course with the wrong habits, and moving them wastes a decision. A student who cannot hold the algebraic demand of Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level after a term of real work may genuinely be in the wrong room.

The constraint that should not be forgotten is the university requirement. Engineering, physics, mathematics and many economics programmes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, so a move can close doors that matter in two years. Read the specific programme pages for the universities under consideration before the decision, rather than relying on a general rule or on what a cousin was told about a different country's system.

sections.heading: Availability, cost and the thin local pool
paragraphs: Finishing the proximity question honestly: IB students are around 7 per cent of Dubai's private-school enrolment against 37 per cent on UK curricula, per Dubai Media Office figures for 2024-25. A minority programme spread across a city of 227 private schools does not produce a concentration of Higher Level maths specialists at the outer edge of Dubailand.

Availability is tightest in Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, particularly for Paper 3 work in the weeks before mocks, when every Diploma family in Dubai wants the same thing at the same time. Where we cannot cover a request in the window you want, you get the slots that exist, an honest estimate of when the preferred window may open, or a recommendation to look elsewhere. A general maths tutor is not placed into a Paper 3 request.

On price, published figures: an IB specialist online is AED 200 to 450 or more an hour, with TutorChase at AED 270, Unitors publishing IB from AED 200 and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table at AED 200 to 450+. A qualified subject tutor at AED 150 to 300 covers Standard Level competently. In-home visits run AED 180 to 500 including travel, per Bestimate at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500, with Serena at the upper end because the round trip is eighty to a hundred and twenty minutes.

For maths specifically the in-home premium buys unusually little, because the subject's working surface is a page of algebra and a graph. On a shared screen both people write, both keep the annotated file, and graphs can be plotted live so a student sees what changing a parameter does. What the room does need is paper, pencil and the physical graphing calculator, since calculator technique is examined and an emulator is not the same instrument.

faqs.question: How do I find out which IB maths course my child is taking?
faqs.answer: The school's option confirmation names it: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, at Higher or Standard Level. It is worth checking rather than assuming, because the four courses differ in paper structure, calculator access and the command terms that dominate. Quote the course to any tutor you contact before anything else — it is the difference between a first session that starts work and three sessions spent establishing what is being studied. If the school's wording is unclear, the Diploma coordinator will confirm it.

faqs.question: Which IB maths papers allow a graphing calculator?
faqs.answer: All of them except Analysis and Approaches Paper 1, which is sat without one — that is the only non-calculator paper across the suite at Standard Level, and Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level also sits a paper without a calculator. Applications and Interpretation permits a calculator throughout both papers. The consequence is that the two routes examine opposite habits: hand fluency with surds, logarithms and exact values on one side, documented calculator use and interpretation on the other.

faqs.question: What does 'hence' mean in an IB maths question?
faqs.answer: It obliges the student to use the previous result. A correct answer obtained by a different method can lose marks when the question said 'hence', which students find unfair until they see it in a mark scheme. The related terms matter just as much: 'show that' means the answer is given and the derivation is the mark; 'write down' signals that no working is expected; 'verify' means substitute and confirm rather than solve from scratch. Misreading these costs marks before the mathematics is examined.

faqs.question: Why does Paper 3 matter so much at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Because it is sixty minutes for 20 per cent of the grade and it tests something the other papers do not: sustained reasoning across a scaffolded investigation. It cannot be passed by recognising familiar question types, which is why doing more Paper 1 practice does not prepare anyone for it. Most students meet far too few Paper 3 questions before their mock, so the first one they attempt seriously is under examination conditions. It needs its own allocation in a plan rather than the last ten minutes of a session.

faqs.question: What are the five Exploration criteria worth in IB maths?
faqs.answer: Against five criteria totalling twenty marks and worth 20 per cent of the subject grade: presentation four, mathematical communication four, personal engagement three, reflection three, and use of mathematics six. Criterion E, use of mathematics, decides the ceiling because it assesses whether the mathematics is relevant, correct and sophisticated enough for the course level. That is why topic viability must be tested before any work begins — a thin topic caps the grade however well the piece is written.

faqs.question: How much Exploration help can a Serena tutor legitimately give?
faqs.answer: A tutor can test whether a topic the student has proposed contains enough mathematics to score on Criterion E, explain each criterion, question the reasoning and give feedback on a draft the student wrote. A tutor cannot choose the topic and hand it over, write or rewrite text, produce or process data, or supply a previous student's Exploration as a model. Those are passing off another person's work as the student's own, which is misconduct under IB rules and risks the whole Diploma rather than one grade.

faqs.question: What separates a 5 from a 7 in IB maths?
faqs.answer: At a 5, students usually know the content and lose marks in volume to four habits: method not shown, command terms misread, calculator answers given without input or interpretation, and questions abandoned when a step fails. All four are visible in a marked paper and close in four to six sessions of strict marking. Reaching a 7 needs something else — fluency under time pressure and sustained reasoning across extended questions, which is why timed practice and, at Higher Level, Paper 3 work matter more at the top.

faqs.question: My child chose Applications and Interpretation expecting it to be easier. Was that wrong?
faqs.answer: Partly. Applications and Interpretation is a different course rather than a lighter one, and at Higher Level it carries substantial breadth including matrices, graph theory and demanding statistics that students choosing it for an easier life do not expect. It suits students strong at interpretation, modelling and data, and those students do better in it than they would in Analysis and Approaches. The real constraint is university requirements: engineering, physics and mathematics programmes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level.

faqs.question: Can my child switch maths course or level during DP1?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the school owns the decision because it holds the timetable, the assessment record and the registration. Movement is easiest early in DP1 and becomes harder as content diverges and deadlines approach, with a level change inside the same route usually simpler than a switch between routes. Before deciding, get two marked papers looked at: a student losing marks on method, command terms and timing is in the right course with the wrong habits, and moving them wastes the decision.

faqs.question: Is there an IB maths tutor living near Serena?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but it is the wrong filter. IB students are around 7 per cent of Dubai's private-school enrolment, so Higher Level maths specialists are spread across the city rather than concentrated at the outer edge of Dubailand, and most Serena IB families already travel out of the belt for school. We teach online one-to-one, which removes distance from the question entirely — there is no IB Gram office or centre in the UAE, and home visits are a service we offer only in India.

faqs.question: Does maths tutoring work as well over video?
faqs.answer: For this subject, unusually well. A maths lesson is a shared working surface, and a shared digital one beats a single notebook: both people write on it, both keep the annotated file, and the working from three weeks ago is still there to point at. Graphs can be plotted live so the student sees what changing a parameter does. What the room needs is paper, pencil and the physical graphing calculator, because calculator technique is examined and practising on an emulator is not the same instrument.

faqs.question: What does an IB maths tutor cost around Serena?
faqs.answer: An IB specialist teaching online is quoted at AED 200 to 450 or more an hour, with TutorChase publishing AED 270, Unitors publishing IB from AED 200 and Bestimate's 2026 rate table at AED 200 to 450+. A qualified subject tutor at AED 150 to 300 covers Standard Level competently. In-home visits run AED 180 to 500 including travel, at the upper end for Serena because the round trip is eighty to a hundred and twenty minutes. Those are published market figures; our rate is quoted after the free trial.

faqs.question: When should we start Paper 3 preparation?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most schools get to it, and certainly before the first mock. The problem is not difficulty but unfamiliarity: a student who has attempted two Paper 3 questions will handle the third very differently from one meeting the format under examination conditions. In DP1 an introduction of two or three questions is enough to remove the shock; the sustained work belongs in DP2 alongside content. Availability for Paper 3 coaching is tightest in the weeks before mocks, when every Dubai family wants it at once.

faqs.question: Is a government permit needed to tutor maths privately in Serena?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and, according to u.ae, is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18, applying through MoHRE's Private Tutor Licensing service. Because the permit is free, no tutor should pass on a licensing cost, and since no fine schedule is published, treat any penalty figure quoted at you as unverified.

Send them and you will get that answer plus a free first lesson with the tutor who would continue. Teaching is live, one-to-one and online on Gulf Standard Time, and nobody drives to Al Qudra Road.
